title: Site-defined Cu-O ensembles enable hydrogen-conserving light-driven ethane upgrading

paper_content.abstract: Upgrading light alkanes to value-added olefins is a long-standing challenge, owing to the high stability of C–H bonds and the tendency for overoxidation at elevated temperatures. Here, we introduce a light-driven strategy for ethane dehydrogenation using Cu-doped TiO , in which atomically dispersed Cu coordinated to bridging oxygen (O ) creates well-defined [Cu–O] ensembles that orchestrate site-specific, stepwise C–H activation. Photogenerated holes localize at O sites to initiate the first C–H cleavage, while adjacent Cu centers mediate β–H elimination and H evolution. In contrast, trace β–H activation at O sites generates *H species that cannot desorb due to a prohibitive coupling barrier with *H on O , leading to Cu reduction and progressive deactivation. Co-feeding CO restores the active Cu coordination environment and suppresses this deactivation process without perturbing the primary reaction pathway. This cooperative design achieves a C H production rate of 21.1 mmol g-1 h-1 with nearly stoichiometric H evolution and a quantum efficiency of 6.1% under 365 nm irradiation. These findings establish a site-defined, hydrogen-conserving route for photocatalytic alkane upgrading, offering a general blueprint for selective C–H bond transformations with long-term stability.
paper_content.introduction:
With increasing demands for carbon neutrality and cleaner chemical production, the selective upgrading of light alkanes, key components of shale gas, into value-added chemicals has become a strategic goal in sustainable catalysis1-5. Among these alkanes, ethane (C H ), the second most abundant constituent (5–20 vol%) of shale gas, represents a promising feedstock for on-demand ethylene (C H ) production, given its availability, low cost, and the central role of C H in the global petrochemical supply chain6-9. However, catalytic ethane dehydrogenation (EDH) to ethylene remains fundamentally challenging due to the high bond dissociation energy of its C–H bonds (~415 kJ/mol) and the inherent difficulty in achieving high selectivity under practical conditions10-14.

In thermocatalytic systems, C–H activation typically proceeds via either noble metal nanoparticles (e.g., Pt, Pd) or via lattice oxygen species in reducible metal oxides such as ZnO, NiO, or CeO 13-17. These processes generally require elevated temperatures (600–800°C) to surmount the kinetic barrier for C–H cleavage18-20. Such harsh conditions often induce sintering of metal particles, excessive carbon deposition from deep dehydrogenation, and more critically, difficulties in regulating the properties, reactivity, and regeneration kinetics of active lattice oxygen21-25. The resulting active oxygen species are prone to uncontrolled spillover, which not only promotes nonselective overoxidation but also accelerates the consumption of valuable H during O - or CO - assisted regeneration via H O formation13,15,26. These issues fundamentally limit the atom- and energy-efficiency of thermocatalytic EDH (TEDH) processes and create a trade-off between activity, selectivity, and catalyst longevity.

Photocatalytic EDH (PEDH) has emerged as a promising low-temperature alternative that can harness photogenerated charge carriers to circumvent the thermodynamic and kinetic limitations of thermocatalysis12,27-38. Metal oxide systems such as LaMn Cu O and heterojunction catalysts like PdZn/ZnO have demonstrated light-assisted C–H activation through lattice oxygen participation or heterojunction-driven charge separation31,33. These successes underscore the viability of photocatalytic strategies in achieving energy-efficient alkane conversion. However, several key challenges remain unresolved. First, most photocatalytic systems suffer from low C H selectivity due to overoxidation by highly reactive oxygen species such as •OH or •O -, which indiscriminately cleave both C–H and C–C bonds12,34,39. Second, the formation, dynamics, and reactivity of surface hydrogen species (*H) remain poorly understood, especially their role in surface poisoning and deactivation16,40. Third, the lack of atomic-level control over the geometry of active sites and their redox cooperativity hampers the precise mediation of sequential hydrogen abstraction steps without undesired side reactions.

Herein, we address these challenges with a photocatalytic platform based on Cu-doped TiO , where atomically dispersed Cu bridged by oxygen (O ) forms site-defined [Cu–O] ensembles that serve as the primary centers for sequential C–H activation and H evolution. Photogenerated holes localize at O to trigger the first C–H cleavage in C H , while the adjacent Cu center promotes β–H elimination with concurrent H release. In contrast, β–H activation at Ti-bonded bridging oxygen (O ) generates *H species that are kinetically trapped in H evolution, leading to Cu reduction and catalyst deactivation. Co-feeding CO promotes the removal of *H from these non-cooperative O sites, preserving the active [Cu–O] ensembles without disturbing the primary dehydrogenation route. This light-driven, site-defined strategy achieves highly selective C H production with minimal H loss, offering an atom- and energy-efficient blueprint for sustainable alkane upgrading.
paper_content.results:
Photocatalyst preparation and characterizations
Figure 1a illustrates the synthetic route for anchoring single Cu atoms on TiO (denoted as Cu /TiO ) via a previously reported MIL-125(Ti)-templated pre-encapsulation strategy41. Initially, MIL-125 with Ti vacancies (Ti v ) was synthesized, exhibiting a smooth disc-like morphology (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 1a). Upon impregnation with Cu2+, the Ti sites were occupied to form the Cu/MIL-125 intermediate, and a slight structural collapse occurred due to the polar solvent effect (Fig. 1c). Subsequent calcination of Cu/MIL-125 at 500 °C in air yielded the final Cu /TiO catalyst (Fig. 1d), with the (101) facet of anatase TiO 2 exposed (Supplementary Fig. 1b). Additionally, a slight increase in Ti3+, oxygen vacancies (V ), and surface hydroxyl groups (–OH) is observed after the introduction of lower-valent Cu (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) confirmed the complete removal of organic linkers, as only adsorbed water loss below 200°C was observed with no additional weight loss up to 800°C (Supplementary Fig. 2). More detailed synthetic procedures are provided in the Methods.

Inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry determined a Cu loading of 1.4 wt% in Cu /TiO . Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Fig. 1e) confirm the formation of MOF intermediates and anatase TiO , while the absence of Cu-related diffraction peaks in both Cu/MIL-125 and Cu /TiO indicates that the MOF-based pre-encapsulation strategy effectively produces highly dispersed Cu species. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping (Fig. 1f) further showed the uniform distribution of Cu. High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) image reveals isolated bright spots corresponding to single Cu atoms (Fig. 1g). Atomic intensity profiles (Fig. 1h) from two representative regions show distinct contrast between Ti and Cu, and the equidistant arrangement (ca. 0.35 nm) of Ti and Cu atoms in region 2 provides direct evidence that individual Cu atoms are anchored on TiO by substituting Ti sites.

The oxidation states of Cu were analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). As shown in Fig. 2a, a distinct satellite peak confirms the presence of Cu2+, which is further verified by electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 3)42. Deconvolution of the Cu 2p spectrum reveals two characteristic peaks at binding energy (B.E.) of 933.64 eV (62%) and 932.42 eV (38%). The former is assigned to Cu2+ and the latter to Cu+, as confirmed by the valence-sensitive Cu LMM Auger spectra. Specifically, the Cu LMM spectrum of Cu /TiO exhibits a kinetic energy shift toward the Cu+ position relative to the CuO reference (Fig. 2b).

X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) measurements were performed to elucidate the local coordination environment of Cu sites in Cu /TiO . In the Cu K-edge XANES spectrum, the white-line peak intensity of Cu /TiO falls between those of CuO and Cu O (Fig. 2c), indicating an average Cu oxidation state between +1 and +2, consistent with the XPS results. Fourier-transformed EXAFS spectra in R-space (Fig. 2d) reveal a single peak corresponding to the first-shell Cu–O scattering, with no detectable Cu–Cu or Cu–(O)–Cu contributions. Wavelet transform analysis (Fig. 2e) further confirms this assignment, showing a dominant Cu–O feature at approximately 1.5 Å (R-space) and 4.4 Å⁻¹ (k-space), distinct from the Cu–Cu signature of metallic Cu foil at ~2.1 Å and 7.1 Å⁻¹. Furthermore, the O K-edge XANES spectrum of Cu /TiO retains the characteristic crystal field profile of TiO (Fig. 2f), exhibiting resolved absorption features at 529–536 eV and 536–548 eV regions that are assigned to electronic transitions from O 1s to O 2p–Ti/Cu 3d and O 2p–Ti/Cu 4s4p hybridized orbitals43,44, respectively. Within the 3d–hybridization region, crystal-field splitting yields well-defined t and e peaks, with the t /e ratio serving as a sensitive probe of electron occupancy in 3d orbitals45,46. As evidenced in Supplementary Figs. 5a and 5b, Cu /TiO exhibits a lower t /e ratio than undoped TiO , signifying enhanced electron accumulation in t orbitals. Considering the contrasting 3d electron configurations of Cu2+ (d9) and Ti4+ (d0) (Supplementary Fig. 5c), this reduction directly evidences Cu–O orbital hybridization. Concurrently, the overall attenuation of absorption intensity of Cu /TiO (Fig. 2f) further confirms the incorporation of Cu into the TiO lattice, rather than being surface-dangling, consistent with our HAADF-STEM observations (Fig. 1g). EXAFS fitting was used to further extract the quantitative spatial configuration of Cu atoms (Fig. 2g and Supplementary Table 1). The results indicate an average Cu coordination number of 3.6, suggesting the probable presence of 60% [Cu–O ] and 40% [Cu–O ] coordination units. These ratios correspond well with the concentrations of Cu2+ and Cu+ determined by XPS analysis, respectively. The quantitative agreement between XPS and XAS spectral analyses unambiguously confirms the near 100% accessibility of Cu active sites, representing exceptional atomic utilization efficiency. Taken together, we assign [Cu–O ] as the predominant configuration for Cu2+ species, while [Cu–O ] corresponds to Cu+ sites. To further evaluate the generality of this MOF-based pre-encapsulation strategy for synthesizing single-atom catalysts, we additionally prepared Ag/TiO under identical synthetic conditions. HAADF-STEM images of Ag/TiO display isolated bright spots that can be assigned to individual Ag atoms, and the corresponding Ag K-edge EXAFS spectra show Ag–O coordination without any detectable Ag–Ag or Ag–(O)–Ag paths (Supplementary Fig. 6). These results, together with the atomically dispersed Cu centers in Cu /TiO , strongly support that the present synthesis method is capable of stabilizing different metals predominantly in single-atom states.

Performance evaluation of PEDH
The PEDH experiments were carried out in a sealed quartz reactor under xenon lamp irradiation without extra heating. Infrared thermal imaging and thermocouple measurements indicated a catalyst surface temperature of approximately 108℃. (Supplementary Fig. 7). As shown in Fig. 3a, bare TiO exhibited negligible activity, whereas metal deposition (Cu, Au, Ag, Pd, and Pt) significantly altered the reaction pathway. Specifically, Au- and Ag-loaded TiO surfaces predominantly generated C H via C H coupling, while Pd- and Pt-loaded surfaces produced primarily H through deep dehydrogenation, accompanied by carbon deposition (Supplementary Fig. 8). In striking contrast, Cu /TiO demonstrated dramatically enhanced near-stoichiometric production of C H and H with 97% C H selectivity, highlighting efficient and controlled selective dehydrogenation to C H at the localized [Cu–O] sites. Switching the feed gas from C H to C H /H or C H /H (over-dehydrogenation product) yielded no significant products, further indicating that, under the present conditions, [Cu–O] sites show low intrinsic activity toward side reactions, including alkene hydrogenation and over-dehydrogenation (Supplementary Fig. 9). Furthermore, under a fixed coating area (~3.14 cm2), the mass-specific C H and H yields displayed pronounced catalyst dosage dependence (Fig. 3b), arising from limited photon penetration depth that restricts effective light absorption and prevents the lower catalyst layers from being fully utilized. Given that photothermal effects generally exhibit greater penetration depth than photoexcitation effects47,48, light-induced heating was consequently excluded as the primary performance contributor, supported by dark control experiments at the same catalyst surface temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 10a). However, when an ice bath was introduced under constant light intensity to attenuate the photothermal effect, the photocatalytic yield decreased from 8.4 to 3.8 mmol g-1 h-1 while the product selectivity remained unchanged, clearly demonstrating that the light-induced thermal effect (that is, phonon) plays an important synergistic role in the reaction. Moreover, the linear correlation of C H production with light intensity and wavelength-dependent PEDH performance further collectively establish the photon-driven and phonon-assisted mechanism of PEDH over a Cu /TiO (Supplementary Figs. 10b and 10c).

Remarkably, this system achieved an exceptionally high C H yield of 21.1 mmol g-1 h-1 (Fig. 3b) with an apparent quantum efficiency (AQY) of 6.1% at 365 nm (Supplementary Fig. 10d and Supplementary Table 2), surpassing state-of-the-art photothermal EDH systems at 650°C and achieving the highest reported efficiency among non-O PEDH systems to date (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Table 3)12,32-38,49-52.

The operational stability of the catalyst was evaluated by monitoring the time-dependent cumulative C H yield under prolonged reaction conditions. In a C H atmosphere, a nonlinear accumulation of C H over 240 min indicated gradual catalyst deactivation (Fig. 3d), despite the carbon balance remaining close to 1.0. This deactivation correlates with a macroscopic color change of the catalyst from light green to dark blue, as well as a decrease in the Cu2+ signal detected by in situ EPR (Supplementary Fig. 11a). Critically, this deactivation and the change in Cu2+ content could be effectively mitigated by CO co-feeding (Fig. 3d), indicating that the structural changes of the Cu active sites are reversible and that Cu2+ ([Cu-O ]) is likely a potential active center. However, the observed color change under reaction conditions cannot be simply attributed to the reduction of Cu2+ via photogenerated electron capture. As a critical control, under an Ar atmosphere, a comparable decrease in the Cu2+ signal is observed without any noticeable macroscopic color change (Supplementary Fig. 11b). This clear contrast indicates that the color evolution observed in reactive atmospheres does not arise solely from changes in the Cu valence state. The origin of these valence-state variations and their relationship to the reversible structural evolution of the Cu sites will be discussed in detail in the following sections. In addition, to clarify that the observed catalyst deactivation is not an artifact arising from the use of a sealed batch reactor, a series of supplementary control experiments were conducted. First, although a slight pressure increase is detected in the sealed system during the reaction, its magnitude consistently remains below 10% of the initial pressure, and its influence on the reaction kinetics can therefore be considered negligible (Supplementary Fig. 12). Second, the stabilizing role of CO and the intrinsic durability of the catalyst were further verified under continuous-flow conditions. While pronounced deactivation is observed in a C H /Ar atmosphere (Supplementary Fig. 13), the C H production rate is maintained at over 95% of its initial value during 20 h of operation in a C H /CO atmosphere (Fig. 3e). Meanwhile, HAADF-STEM analysis of the post-reaction catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 14) confirmed the preserved atomic dispersion of Cu species without detectable aggregation.

Temperature-programmed surface reaction (TPSR) studies in C H /CO and C H atmospheres elucidated thermal dehydrogenation pathways. Both systems exhibited identical reaction onset temperatures around 505°C (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 15a), consistent with TEDH activity profiles (Supplementary Fig. 15b), indicating that C H activation governs reaction initiation and serves as the rate-determining step. Stability evaluation of Cu /TiO for TEDH at 550°C revealed low initial activity (ca. 1.2 mmol g-1 h-1) with rapid deactivation to 20% of the initial activity within 10 h (Fig. 3g). Notably, compared with the aforementioned PEDH processes under continuous-flow conditions, this TEDH process exhibits higher H yields than C H yields alongside substantial carbon deposition (Fig. 3h), signifying the predominance of deep dehydrogenation side reactions. In contrast, the light-driven selectivity of PEDH enables targeted C–H activation while suppressing deep dehydrogenation and over-oxidation, highlighting the intrinsic advantage of photocatalysis for controlled C H -to-C H conversion.

Mechanistic investigations
A systematic Arrhenius analysis revealed a significant reduction in apparent activation energies (Ea) for photocatalytic and thermal C H activation. The photocatalytic Ea was 24.94 kJ mol-1, representing a 75% decrease compared to thermal catalysis (98.41 kJ mol-1, Fig. 4a), highlighting the enhanced ability of photocatalysis to facilitate C–H bond cleavage. Active species quenching experiments were conducted to further understand the mechanism of efficient C H activation under mild conditions (Fig. 4b). It should be noted that, to avoid interference arising from the quenchers themselves occupying catalyst surface sites or altering surface properties, two different quenchers were employed for each target species (h+ or e-) for cross-validation. The quenching efficiencies of all scavengers toward photogenerated electrons and holes were confirmed by photoluminescence spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 16). Specifically, when ferrocene (C H Fe) and sodium oxalate (Na C O ) were introduced as hole (h⁺) scavengers, the yields of C H and H decreased in an equimolar manner, indicating that h⁺ predominantly participates in the initial step, namely the cleavage of the first C–H bond of C H . In contrast, when potassium persulfate (K S O ) and potassium dichromate (K Cr O ) were introduced as electron (e⁻) scavengers, the C H /H ratio markedly deviated from the theoretical value of 1.0 and increased to 4.7 and 5.0, respectively, demonstrating that e⁻ plays a crucial role in promoting the kinetics of H formation. Meanwhile, quenching e⁻ led to a >90% decrease in the total product yield, which likely implies that the accumulation of *H species on the catalyst surface blocks active sites and ultimately causes catalyst deactivation. To further elucidate the role of Cu sites in the reaction, NH was introduced into the system to coordinate with Cu, forming Cu–NH complexes and thereby specifically blocking the Cu sites; this blocking effect was verified by NH –TPD measurements (Supplementary Fig. 17). The results show that the decrease in C H yield is more pronounced than that of H , and the additional decrease in C H (relative to H ) is stoichiometrically correlated with the formation of C H . This correspondence indicates that, once Cu sites are occupied, the reaction pathway leading to C H is effectively suppressed, and a fraction of the reaction intermediates is diverted toward a C–C coupling pathway to form C H . Accordingly, we propose that atomically dispersed Cu sites predominantly mediate β–H activation, thereby driving the dehydrogenation of the *C H intermediate to form C H . Once these Cu sites are blocked, the lack of accessible active sites for further dehydrogenation may lead to the accumulation and prolonged residence of *C H species on the catalyst surface, which in turn is more likely to promote C–C coupling pathways and ultimately yield C H . Highly sensitive synchrotron-based vacuum ultraviolet-photoionization mass spectrometry (SVUV-PIMS) was employed to detect trace gaseous intermediates, observing signals at m/z = 28.031 and 29.037 under the C H atmosphere (Fig. 4c). Detailed analysis of the corresponding scanning photoionization efficiency (PIE) curve revealed well-defined ionization onsets at 10.40 eV and 8.18 eV (Supplementary Fig. 18), respectively, which unambiguously identified these species as C H (IE=10.40 eV) and •C H (IE=8.24 eV) based on their characteristic ionization energy (IE) thresholds53,54, with quantitative analysis indicating that 9.5% of the signal intensity at m/z=29.037 originated from C H isotopologues.

Further experiments were employed to elucidate the interaction between photogenerated carriers and reactant molecules. First, we compared in situ femtosecond transient absorption spectra (fs-TAS) of the Cu /TiO under different atmospheres using the 365 nm pump laser as the light source (Figs. 4d and 4e). Under Ar conditions, Cu /TiO presents TiO -like characteristic negative peaks at ca. 380 nm (Supplementary Fig. 19a), which are identified as the ground-state bleaching (GSBC) signals of TiO and provide insights into the population of photoelectrons in its conduction band (CB)55,56. Compared to pristine TiO , Cu /TiO exhibits a weaker GSB signal, indicating fewer electrons at its CB, likely due to Cu sites acting as shallow traps that capture photoexcited e-. By analyzing the recovery kinetics of the GSB signal, two distinct lifetimes were identified. The shorter lifetime (τ ) corresponds to the trapping of photogenerated e- from the CB of TiO into Cu sites, while the longer lifetime (τ ) is attributed to the recombination of electrons in the CB with holes in the valence band (VB) of TiO 57,58. The prolonged τ observed in Cu /TiO compared to pristine TiO indicates that electron transfer to Cu sites effectively delays charge recombination with VB holes, thereby extending the charge carrier lifetime (Supplementary Fig. 19b). Transient photocurrent measurements and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) further confirm enhanced charge separation efficiency (Supplementary Fig. 20). Notably, under C H exposure, Cu /TiO exhibits enhanced GSB intensity with accelerated decay kinetics (Figs. 4d and 4e), indicating ethane's dual role as electron donor and acceptor. Specifically, adsorbed C H molecules consume photogenerated holes in the VB (i.e., injecting electrons into the VB). This process facilitates the transition from the ground to the excited state and increases the initial electron concentration in the CB, thereby enhancing the GSB signal. Meanwhile, the generated •C H promotes electron consumption by forming H through *H species, which arise from Cu-mediated β–H bond activation, further accelerating charge carrier dynamics. Besides, in situ time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy (TRFL) was also conducted under different atmospheres. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 21 and Supplementary Table 4, the average carrier lifetime was extended from 2.09 ns to 6.07 ns after Cu loading, demonstrating effective suppression of carrier recombination. It is particularly noteworthy that upon switching the reaction atmosphere to C H , the carrier lifetime dramatically decreased to 4.12 ns. This observation directly verifies that the photogenerated carriers migrating to the catalyst surface undergo rapid redox reactions with C H molecules.

Subsequently, the distribution of photogenerated carriers under light irradiation was further investigated using in situ XPS. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 22, the Cu 2p peak is shifted toward lower B.E. while the O 1s peak is shifted toward higher B.E. under light irradiation, indicating that the e- and h+ tend to be localized in the Cu and O sites, respectively. Further theoretical analysis of the partial density of states (PDOS) for Cu /TiO and TiO reveals that Cu /TiO generates gap states originating from Cu d-orbitals compared to TiO , which theoretically confirms that the doped Cu sites act as shallow electron-trapping centers (Fig. 4f). Based on the above mechanistic evidence, we propose the reaction mechanism as follows. The C–H bond activation of C H through photogenerated holes constitutes the critical step for initiating the reaction, generating •C H . Subsequently, these •C H undergo dehydrogenation at adjacent Cu sites, releasing C H and adsorbed *H species. The accumulated *H species are then reduced via photogenerated electrons, culminating in the evolution of H . Notably, in the aforementioned in situ TAS and TRFL tests, the CO -induced kinetic decay of charge carriers was negligible versus the accelerated decay driven by C H (Supplementary Figs. 19 and 21). Simultaneously, •C H radical signals showed minimal perturbations under CO co-feeding (Fig. 4c), collectively confirming that C H non-oxidative dehydrogenation remains dominant in the C H /CO mixture. To elucidate the role of CO in stabilizing Cu /TiO described above, product distributions before and after CO introduction were analyzed. As shown in Fig. 4g, trace CO formation was detected only under C H /CO co-feeding, but was absent in the CO -free atmosphere. Control experiments with H /CO co-feeding also yielded no detectable CO, indicating that the catalyst is unable to effectively activate molecular H under the present conditions and thus cannot initiate a redox-mediated reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) pathway. These findings therefore rule out RWGS as the source of CO formation in the C H /CO co-feeding system. Furthermore, C18O isotope labeling experiments confirmed that the oxygen in CO originates from CO rather than from the lattice oxygen (Fig. 4h). To further elucidate the CO formation pathway, we set a baseline feed of C H : CO = 1:1 (20 mL each) and systematically varied the ratio by increasing either reactant. CO production showed a strong positive correlation with C H input (mirroring C H yield), but remained insensitive to CO concentration (Fig. 4i). These findings further support that CO yield is indirectly driven by C H conversion.

Subsequently, in situ near-ambient pressure XPS spectroscopy (NAP-XPS) was employed to monitor the chemical state evolution of Cu /TiO under C H and C H /CO atmospheres, and to elucidate the role of CO . The results revealed that the Cu2+ content decreased significantly under pure C H but was notably suppressed when CO was co-fed (Figs. 5a and 5b), corroborating prior in situ EPR observations (Supplementary Fig. 11) and further implying that Cu2+ ([Cu-O ]) species are closely associated with the catalytically active centers. However, it should be particularly noted that in a C H atmosphere, the transformation of Cu2+ to Cu⁺ is accompanied by an increase in –OH content. In contrast, under CO co-feeding conditions, –OH is significantly consumed. Accordingly, we speculate that under C H atmosphere, the deactivation of the catalyst may be attributed to the coverage of active sites by undissociated *H on lattice oxygen, which leads to the transformation of Cu2+ to Cu+. Besides, quasi-in situ Raman spectroscopy with stepwise feeding of C H and CO revealed that the Eg mode (~144 cm-1) gradually blueshifts with prolonged reaction time in C H atmosphere (Supplementary Fig. 23), indicating enhanced TiO unit cell expansion or strain42. Notably, this blueshift disappears upon switching the atmosphere to CO , further confirming that CO can reverse the microstructural changes induced in Cu /TiO under pure C H conditions.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations on the electronic structure of the Cu /TiO further theoretically revealed the impact of *H adsorption on the Cu valence state. Specifically, adsorption of *H species on lattice oxygen increases the Cu–O bond length from 1.95 Å to 2.26 Å (Supplementary Fig. 24). The charge difference distribution (Supplementary Fig. 25) showed a strong interaction between *H adsorbed on lattice oxygen and the support, with electrons transferring from *H to the Cu site. Bader charge calculations further confirmed that *H coverage reduces the charge at Cu sites (Supplementary Fig. 24 and Supplementary Table 5). In situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) was employed to identify the key reaction intermediates on Cu /TiO under C H and C H /CO atmospheres. Before the DRIFTS measurements, C H temperature-programmed desorption (TPD) experiments were carried out to assess the adsorption behavior. The TPD profiles revealed a markedly enhanced C H adsorption on Cu /TiO compared to bare TiO (Supplementary Fig. 26), confirming [Cu–O] ensembles dominate C H adsorption. Under illumination in C H (Supplementary Fig. 27a), the immediate decay of C H adsorption peaks, accompanied by the simultaneous appearance of *CH CH species and gaseous C H , provided experimental evidence for the stepwise dehydrogenation of C H to C H . Concurrently, the observed generation of –OH indicated *H accumulation on the catalyst surface (Supplementary Fig. 27b). In contrast, CO co-feeding led to the formation of *COOH intermediates (Supplementary Fig. 27c) and the effective suppression of –OH generation (Supplementary Fig. 27d). These results indicate that CO promotes the removal of surface-adsorbed *H species, thereby regenerating the catalytic active sites and concurrently producing CO. This mechanistic insight further corroborates the intrinsic correlation between the CO formation rate and the ethane conversion behavior.

To further validate this mechanism, DFT simulations under the excited/ground-state were employed based on the potential active center model of [Cu–O ]. First, two potential surface bridging oxygen (O ) hole-trapping sites were investigated, which are bonded to Cu and Ti sites respectively and denoted as O and O sites. As revealed in Supplementary Figs. 28 and 29, the hole trapping energies of O and O relative to bulk self-trapped hole were -1.23 and 0.08 eV, confirming effective localization of photogenerated holes at the surface O site. Although Cu was previously confirmed as a shallow electron-trapping center, in subsequent simulations of O -initiated C–H bond activation we placed the photogenerated e- on a remote Ti site to avoid high-energy configurations arising from adjacent electron–hole localization, thereby better reflecting the realistic reaction environment. Critically, Fig. 5c demonstrates that upon hole capture by the O site, the C–H bond of C H undergoes facile cleavage via the hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) mechanism27, with a notably low barrier of 0.46 eV and a negative free energy change (ΔG) of -0.37 eV. This barrier and ΔG are 0.76 eV and 1.16 eV lower than those for ground-state C–H activation at the same O site, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 30), thus serving as a prerequisite for high PEDH activity under mild conditions. This process generates a free •C H radical and an adsorbed *H at the O site. The •C H radical then undergoes two successive mild endergonic steps to transfer a *H to the Cu site via HAT mechanism, involving adsorption at Cu site (0.29 eV) followed by β–H cleavage with a reaction energy of only 0.11 eV. In contrast, although the C–H activation ability of O site is also significantly enhanced after trapping photogenerated holes, with the corresponding barriers being comparable to that at O site, the resulting •C H radical exhibits an adsorption energy of 0.58 eV at the five-coordinated Ti site (Ti ), and the subsequent β–H bond cleavage has a reaction energy as high as 1.60 eV (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 31), both of which are significantly larger than those on the Cu site. This demonstrates that the introduction of Cu not only markedly promotes the efficient localization of photogenerated holes from the bulk to surface O sites, but also facilitates the •C H adsorption and β–H activation capabilities. This synergistic advantage in both hole management and β–H activation underpins the high ethane activation capability and excellent ethylene selectivity of the Cu /TiO catalyst. In addition, the high reaction energy for β–H cleavage at the Cu+ site in [Cu–O ] (1.06 eV) further confirms its limited activity, highlighting [Cu–O ] as the dominant active center (Supplementary Fig. 32). Finally, we calculated the generation of H at the [Cu–O] ensembles assisted by photogenerated e- transferred from nearby Ti sites to Cu, where *H–*H coupling energy barrier is 0.79 eV. Notably, •C H is also possible to continue to activate the β–H bond via hole-trapped O with an energy barrier of 0.07 eV (Supplementary Fig. 33), following the first C–H bond cleavage mechanism. The resulting *H is captured by the O adjacent to [Cu–O] ensembles. Consequently, the H formation is significantly hindered at the O and O sites (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 34), with an energy barrier as high as 2.79 eV. We also considered the possibility of *H migration from the O or O to Cu sites for *H–*H coupling, yet these processes remain challenging. For migration from the O to the Cu site, *H could first relocate to the O site (three-fold coordinated lattice oxygen) with an energy barrier of 1.48 eV, then proceeds from O to the Cu site with a barrier of 3.12 eV (Supplementary Fig. 35), while direct migration from O to the Cu site requires overcoming a 2.92 eV barrier (Supplementary Fig. 36). This indicates that consecutive dehydrogenation on two lattice oxygens leads to difficult desorption of *H, ultimately leading to deactivation of the catalyst due to *H coverage on the [Cu–O ] active sites. Further theoretical calculations (Supplementary Fig. 37) reveal that these two *H species can be transformed into H O via a low energy barrier of 0.40 eV, accompanied by a structural reconstruction from [Cu–O ] to [Cu–O ]. However, this process is still endergonic from a thermodynamic perspective, and the *H species preferentially remain adsorbed on the catalyst surface. Notably, in the presence of CO , CO can cooperatively interact with •C H to form a *COOH intermediate, which promotes the further transformation of the [Cu–O ] species generated during the dehydration process. This, in turn, drives the continuous consumption of the accumulated *H while simultaneously regenerating the [Cu–O ] sites.

Based on the foregoing findings, a light-driven EDH mechanism is delineated in Fig. 5d. Atomically dispersed Cu promotes the localization of photogenerated holes at directly bonded O sites, facilitating initial C–H activation in C H with the significantly reduced energy barriers. The resulting •C H species binds to Cu, where β–H elimination proceeds, and the *H generated is subsequently released as H through the cooperative action of site-defined [Cu–O] ensembles. This sequential dehydrogenation coupled with efficient H evolution accounts for the high activity and selectivity toward C H . In contrast, β–H activation at O sites adjacent to (but not coordinated with) Cu lacks Cu-mediated *H–*H coupling, preventing *H recombination and leading to *H accumulation that poisons active sites. Upon introducing CO , a self-cleaning cycle is established that promotes further transformation of surface *H, thereby removing the *H adlayer and regenerating active sites.
paper_content.methods:
Preparation of catalysts
Synthesis of MIL-125(Tiv). The MIL-125 with Ti vacancies (Ti v ) precursor was synthesized according to the method described in previous literature41. First, 3.0 g of terephthalic acid (99%, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) was dissolved in 54 mL of N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 99.9%, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) with 30 min magnetic stirring at room temperature. Subsequently, 6 mL of methanol (99.9%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) was added and stirred for 5 min, followed by the addition of 1.2 mL of tetrabutyl titanate (TBOT, 99%, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) with additional 5 min stirring. The mixture was transferred to a sealed round-bottom flask and reacted at 130 °C for 20 h under Ar atmosphere using an oil bath. After cooling, the precipitate was collected by centrifugation, successively washed twice with DMF and twice with methanol, and vacuum-dried at 80 °C for 10 h to remove residual solvents, yielding MIL-125(Tiv).

Synthesis of Cu /TiO . 150 mg of MIL-125(Tiv) was dispersed in 50 mL of water/methanol solution (1:4 v/v). Under continuous stirring, a predetermined aliquot of 0.1 M CuCl (99.99%, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) aqueous solution was added dropwise, followed by stirring for 10 h. The resulting mixture was centrifuged and washed thrice with water/methanol solution. After oven-drying at 80 °C, the solid was calcined in a muffle furnace at 500 °C for 4 h with a heating rate of 2 °C/min to obtain Cu /TiO .

Evaluation of catalytic performance
Batch-type performance test. First, the catalyst was uniformly dispersed in 1.0 mL deionized water and coated onto a glass slide (coating area: 3.14 cm2), followed by drying at 80 °C. The catalyst-coated glass slide was placed at the center of the bottom of a sealed 100 mL quartz reactor. To ensure complete replacement of residual air by ethane, the reactor was subjected to three evacuation/ethane-flushing cycles (1 atm, 99.9% C H per cycle) before performance test. A 300 W full-spectrum (250 ~1100 nm) Xe lamp (PLS-SXE300+) was used for vertical irradiation (4 h per reaction) without additional external heating, and the light intensity was monitored using a PL-MW2000 optical power meter. Pressure changes (defined as the difference between the instantaneous pressure and the initial pressure) during the reaction were continuously recorded with an AS511A digital differential manometer (SMART SENSOR). The reaction products were analyzed using a Shimadzu gas chromatograph (GC-2014C) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionization detector (FID). For the C18O 2 isotope-labeled experiment, the gas-phase products were detected by a 7890A-5975C gas chromatography-mass spectrometer (Agilent Technologies Co., Ltd.).

The catalyst surface temperature was simultaneously monitored using a Uti160S infrared thermal imager (UNI-T) and a calibrated K-type thermocouple (diameter 0.25 mm, KAIPUSEN). The thermocouple probe maintained direct contact with the center of the catalyst bed, while the thermal imager was installed at an oblique angle above the reactor, oriented toward the top surface of the catalyst bed to capture thermal image data. The emissivity was established as ε = 0.95 based on an empirical calibration procedure performed with catalyst powder distributed uniformly on a pre-calibrated heating plate. During calibration, the heating plate temperature was systematically varied (50, 100, 150, and 200 °C) and the imager's emissivity setting was adjusted until its temperature readings concurred with the reference values at each point, thereby determining the optimal emissivity value for all subsequent experimental measurements.

Flow-type performance test. The performance tests of flow-type PEDH and TEDH were both evaluated in a PLS-LED 100 photothermal reactor (Beijing Perfectlight) equipped with external temperature control, where the catalyst-bed temperature was monitored by a KE-type thermocouple inserted into the center of the catalyst layer. For each test, 10 mg of catalyst was uniformly coated onto a heat-resistant quartz fiber filter membrane (fixed coating area: 3.14 cm2), and the flow rate of the feed gas (20 vol% C H /20 vol% CO /Ar) was set as 10 mL min-1. The apparent activation energy measurements were carried out in the same reactor, in which a UV light source with fixed intensity was employed to mitigate photothermal effects, and a relatively low temperature window of 60~140 ℃ was selected to ensure that the reaction proceeded in the kinetic regime and to minimize interference from internal and external mass transfer and thermal effects.

The corresponding product yield, selectivity, conversion, and carbon balance were calculated using the following equations:
Yield = [C H ] / (m*t) [1]
Selectivity = [C H ] / ([C H ]+0.5*[CH ]+2*[C H ]) *100% [2]
Conversion = ([C H ] - [C H ]) / [C H ] *100% [3]
Carbon balance = ([C H ]+0.5*[CH ]+2*[C H ]) / [C H ] [4]
where [C H ], [CH ], [C H ] and [C H ] represent the molar amounts of C H , CH , C H and C H , respectively. m and t represent the mass of the catalyst (g) and the reaction time (h), respectively.

Characterization
The morphological characteristics of the samples were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Helios G4 UC), transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Talos F200X), and aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM, Themis Z). Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were acquired using a Rigaku D/MAX 2550 diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.5406 Å), scanning the 2θ range from 5° to 80° at a rate of 8° min-1. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was performed using an ESCALAB 250Xi system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with monochromatic Al Kα radiation (hν=1486.6 eV), and the binding energies were referenced and corrected using the C 1s peak at 284.8 eV. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) measurements were conducted on an Agilent 5800 VDV system. Thermogravimetric/differential thermal analysis (TG/DTA) was conducted using a Netzsch TGA209F1 instrument, with the temperature ranging from 50 to 800 °C. Raman spectroscopy measurements were performed using a Renishaw inVia Raman system, with a 532 nm laser serving as the excitation source. UV-Vis diffuse reflectance spectra of the dry-pressed disk samples were recorded on a Cary 500 spectrophotometer (Varian) with an integrating sphere, using BaSO as a reflectance reference standard. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements were performed using a 100G-18KG/EMX-8/2.7 instrument. Transient photocurrent response and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were conducted using a ZAHNER PP211 electrochemical workstation with a standard three-electrode configuration. The working electrode consisted of fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) glass coated with the sample (5 mg, coating area: 1 cm2), with a platinum counter electrode and a saturated calomel electrode as a reference electrode. Transient photocurrent tests were performed in 0.5 M aqueous Na SO solution, while EIS measurements were carried out in an electrolyte system containing potassium ferricyanide. Ammonia temperature-programmed desorption (NH -TPD) measurements were performed on a Micromeritics AutoChem II 2920 chemisorption analyzer. Following saturation with 10% NH /He gas mixture at 50 °C, the sample was heated from 50 to 800 °C at a rate of 10 °C min-1 under a He flow, while the desorbed gases were monitored via a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). C H -TPD measurements followed an identical procedure to that of NH -TPD, with catalyst saturation achieved via pulsed injection of pure C H gas into the system. Temperature-programmed surface reaction (TPSR) experiments were performed on a TP5080 automatic multi-purpose adsorption analyzer, and the desorbed products were monitored in situ using a Hiden Analytical DECAR mass spectrometer during linear heating from 50 to 800 °C at 10 °C min-1. For C H -TPSR, the feed gas consisted of 20% C H balanced with Ar; for C H /CO -TPSR, the feed gas was composed of 20 vol% C H /20 vol% CO balanced with Ar.

XAFS measurement
Cu K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) was collected in fluorescence mode at the XAFCA beamline of the Singapore Synchrotron Light Source (SSLS). Measurements employed a double-crystal Si (111) monochromator with energy calibration referenced to a Cu foil. O K-edge XAFS measurements were performed at the soft X-ray beamline of the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) (Hefei, China). The XAS data were processed using the Demeter software package (ATHENA and ARTEMIS)59.

In situ experiments
In situ synchrotron-based vacuum ultraviolet-photoionization mass spectrometry (SVUV-PIMS). In situ SVUV-PIMS measurements were conducted at the Atomic and Molecular Physics beamline (BL09U) in the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) (Hefei, China)60. The catalyst was positioned at the center of a laminar flow reactor cell. Reaction products were sampled via molecular beam into the ionization chamber, ionized by synchrotron VUV light, and detected by a time-of-flight mass spectrometer. The experiment began by purging the reaction cell’s differential chamber (pressure stabilized at 20.0 Pa) with 50 vol% C H /Ar at a flow rate of 20 mL min-1 for 30 min to remove air. Illumination was provided by a 300 W xenon lamp (without external heating). Following 30 min of illumination, mass spectra were acquired at 10.5 eV with an integration time of 1000 s. Product photoionization efficiency (PIE) curves were scanned from 8.0 to 11.5 eV with an integration time of 240 s per point. The same procedure was repeated for data collection after switching the feed gas to 50 vol% C H /CO mixture.

In situ femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (fs-TAS). In situ fs-TAS measurements were performed using a Helios spectrometer (Ultrafast system) under pure Ar, 50 vol% C H /Ar, or 50 vol% C H /50 vol%CO . The amplified femtosecond Ti: sapphire laser system operated at a repetition rate of 1 kHz, and the probe light was collected via the lens of an InGaAs diode array.

In-situ time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy (TRFL). In situ TRFL spectra were acquired on an Edinburgh Instruments FLS 980 spectrometer. Samples were sealed in 1 mm-pathlength quartz microcuvettes and measured under pure Ar, C H , or CO atmosphere. Excitation was provided by a 360 nm light-emitting diode (LED) source.

In situ NAP-XPS. In situ NAP-XPS was performed on a Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi system with Al Kα radiation (hν = 1486.6 eV). After Ar⁺ sputtering (3 keV, 40 eV pass energy, 0.1 eV step, 1 min), XPS data under vacuum were first collected, after which 50 vol% C H /Ar or 50 vol% C H /50 vol% CO were continuously introduced. Spectra were recorded sequentially under dark conditions, as well as 20 and 40 min after illumination with a 300 W xenon lamp. NAP-XPS spectra were averaged over 5 scans with charge referencing to C 1s (284.80 eV).

In situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS). In situ DRIFTS measurements were performed on a Thermo Fisher-Nicolet iS20 infrared spectrometer equipped with a liquid nitrogen-cooled mercury-cadmium-telluride (MCT) detector, using a three-window diffuse-reflectance cell (Harrick). Before the test, samples were dehydrated at 120 °C for 1 h. Subsequently, 0.1 g of the dried catalyst was loaded into the sample cell and purged with Ar (99.9 vol%) for 30 min to eliminate surface-adsorbed species. Following Ar purging, a background spectrum was collected under an Ar atmosphere. Ar was then flushed out, and a continuous flow of reactant gas (either 20 vol% C H /Ar or 20 vol% C H /20 vol% CO /Ar) was introduced at a flow rate of 20 mL min-1. Spectra were collected at specified time intervals after initiating light irradiation. The spectral resolution was 4 cm-1, and the scanning range was 4000–600 cm-1.

Theoretical calculations
All spin-polarized calculations were performed with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional within the generalized gradient approximation using the VASP 6.3.2 code61,62. The valence electronic states were expanded in plane-wave basis sets with an energy cutoff at 450 eV, and the occupancy of the one-electron states was calculated using the Gaussian smearing with SIGMA = 0.05 eV. The on-site Hubbard U term (PBE+U) was added for O orbitals and Ti orbitals with a value of 4.0 eV and 4.2 eV to facilitate the localization of trapped holes and electrons. In particular, the U correction on the O 2p orbitals helps to cancel self-interaction errors and enables a more realistic localization of photogenerated holes on surface O sites. In addition, to simplify the treatment of the photoexcited system by excluding the uncertain electron–hole interactions that depend on the specific trapping center, while simultaneously preserving the charge neutrality of the periodic slab and avoiding artificial background-charge corrections, an -OH group was introduced on the bottom surface as an electron acceptor63. To validate the accuracy of the DFT+U method64, complementary HSE06 hybrid functional calculations were systematically performed for all reaction steps, with corresponding energy values exclusively derived from the HSE0627. Structure optimizations were performed using the Quasi-Newton Broyden minimization scheme until the atomic forces on each ion were less than 0.05 eV/Å. The transition states (TSs) were searched using a constrained optimization scheme65. In this approach, we keep the C–H bond distance fixed at preselected values, and minimize the total energy with respect to all remaining orthogonal degrees of freedom. In practice, this allows the adsorbed molecules to rotate and translate under the imposed constraint, and the TiO surface is fully relaxed. A transition state is identified when the forces on all atoms vanish and the total energy exhibits a maximum along the chosen reaction coordinate while remaining a minimum with respect to all other degrees of freedom.

A 4-layer p (2×3) unit cell of 10.3 Å, 11.4 Å with a 20.0 Å vacuum between the slabs in the z direction was used for the construction of the anatase TiO (101) surface. The Brillouin zone was sampled with a 3×2×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh. The free energy calculations are based on Eq.5: ΔG=ΔE+ΔZPE-ΔTS [5] where E is the calculated total energy of the model, ZPE is the change of zero-point vibrational enthalpy, and TS is the entropy. For adsorbed intermediates, vibrational frequencies were calculated at the optimized geometries and used to obtain ΔZPE and the vibrational contribution to ΔS at 383 K. The ΔG corrections were then evaluated using the VASPKIT post-processing tool based on these vibrational frequencies66. For gas-phase species, translational, rotational and vibrational entropy contributions at 383 K were taken from standard thermochemical data (NIST).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, the authors reported an investigation of synthesis of single atom Cu-loaded on TiO2 for photocatalytic ethane dehydrogenation with or without CO2. In the work, the authors carried out a comprehensive investigation on the catalytic performance and mechanism. From the experimental tests and DFT calculation, the authors have presented a clear mechanism on the photocatalysis. The work is innovation and provide new information on the catalytic system. It can be published after revision.
1. The authors prepared several different metal-loaded catalysts and found that these catalysts presented various activity. However, they did not discuss the underline reason. It would be better for the authors to check if all the catalysts are single-atom catalysts.
2. In the work, the authors suggested two Cu species in Cu/TiO2, Cu-O4 and Cu-O3. What are the detailed roles of these species in catalysis?
3. In the tests, the authors found that CO production showed strong positive correlation with C2H6 but remained insensitive to CO2, suggesting CO yield is indirectly driven by C2H6 conversion. How?
4. In DFT calculation, the authors did not check the CO2 involvement on catalysis. It is highly required for the authors to check the role of CO2 in photocatalysis.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Photocatalytic ethane dehydrogenation is a promising route to value-added chemicals, but progress remains limited by low productivity. This study reports a Cu/TiO₂ catalyst with encouraging performance, supported by in-situ characterizations and DFT. The manuscript is clearly written and potentially insightful. At first glance, the work appears to deliver a major advance in activity; however, the activity is overstated and the interpretation is not sufficiently critical. The actual gains require more cautious evaluation. Substantial issues must be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication, with particular emphasis on significantly strengthening the mechanistic analysis. Below are the detailed concerns:
1. From the XPS results, no Cu⁰ exists in the samples. The distributed Cu⁰ shown in Fig. 2A should be removed. The authors report 61% Cu²⁺ and 38% Cu⁺, which is not a minor Cu⁺ fraction. However, they state that “Cu species predominantly exists as Cu²⁺ with minor Cu⁺ states.”.
2. The activity evaluation relies mainly on a batch reactor, yet the Batch-type performance test section does not report the pressure. In a sealed batch reactor the pressure evolves during reaction and this can inflate apparent activity. Please report initial and final pressures, and how pressure changes over time. In addition, surface temperature measurement needs clarification. Please specify the measurement method, the emissivity used for infrared measurements, and the calibration procedure. Different emissivity values can lead to large differences in the measured temperature.
3. Batch and flow data in Table S3 should not be compared directly. Batch often overstates activity relative to flow, as your Fig. 3E shows. Please give apple to apple comparisons. Compare batch with batch and flow with flow, and test Cu/TiO₂ in a flow reactor under C₂H₆/Ar, including a stability test. Flow performance is the key metric for industrial relevance.
4. The methods state that a 300 W Xe lamp (PLS-SXE300+) was used for vertical irradiation for 4 h without additional heating. Please clarify how activity was calculated for each rate. There is a discrepancy between Fig. 3B and Fig. 3D. In Fig. 3B, even with 10 mg catalyst, the reported rate is about 7 mmol h⁻¹ g⁻¹. In Fig. 3D under C₂H₆/Ar, the accumulated amount after 4 h is about 5.5 mmol g⁻¹, which corresponds to about 1.1 mmol h⁻¹ g⁻¹. In addition, please report the ethane conversion and the carbon balance under C2H6/Ar and C2H6/CO2/Ar.
5. In Figure S9B, the activities were measured with a 777 mW cm⁻² xenon lamp and 10 mg catalyst. When the light intensity is about 310 mW cm⁻², the C₂H₄ yield in the figure is only around 1.1 mmol h⁻¹ g⁻¹. “yield” appears misspelled in the figure. In Figure S9C, the activity drops by only about 10% when wavelengths <400 nm are used, and there is no activity when wavelengths > 400 nm are used. However, in Table S2 at 365 nm with an intensity of only 54 mW cm⁻² and 50 mg catalyst, the reported C₂H₄ amount is 0.057 mmol h⁻¹. This corresponds to about 1.14 mmol h⁻¹ g⁻¹. Is this possible?
6. The description of AQY conditions is inconsistent. The caption of Fig. S9A states “UV–visible diffuse reflectance spectra and corresponding AQY values of Cu₁/TiO₂ after 1 h of irradiation with different monochromatic lights. Default conditions: 10 mg catalyst, 1 atm pure C₂H₆, 777 mW cm⁻² xenon lamp, 4 h test, batch reactor.” In contrast, Table S2 states “The AQY measurements were conducted in a sealed quartz reactor using 50 mg of catalyst uniformly coated over a 1.0 cm radius circular area for a 1 h reaction.” Please ensure the accuracy of all data.
7. The authors state that “these findings further support that CO yield is indirectly driven by C₂H₆ conversion, with CO₂ serving solely as the oxygen source.” The observed C₂H₄/H₂ ratio is close to 1, which is consistent with non-oxidative dehydrogenation. If CO₂ provides only oxygen, please clarify where the carbon in the produced CO comes from. Please calculate the full carbon balance. Conduct ¹³C labeling to confirm the source of carbon.
8. What temperature was used for the Ea calculation under illumination? Was the photothermal effect excluded?
9. Cu/TiO₂ is widely reported for RWGS. Why was no CO detected in the H₂/CO₂ control experiment?
10. In the NAP-XPS results, what changes are observed in Ti?
11. In the DFT section, the reported barrier reduction of 62.3% for C–H activation at the same Obr Cu site in Path 1 (1.22 eV to 0.46 eV) is clear. Please explain how the percentages 94.1%, 96.6%, and 71.7% were obtained for Paths 2, 3, and 4. For example, Path 4 is listed as 2.83 eV to 0.83 eV, which gives about 70.7% if computed as (2.83-0.83)/2.83, not 71.7%.
12. In the dark-state DRIFTS experiments with C₂H₆ and CO₂, gas-phase C₂H₆ shows bands in the same region as surface species. The observed signals may therefore originate from gas-phase C₂H₆ rather than adsorbates. On this basis, the conclusion of preferential C₂H₆ adsorption over CO₂ is not supported. Please perform CO₂-DRIFTS and competitive C₂H₆/CO₂ adsorption.
13. Figure S24 shows only the infrared spectrum of Cu₁/TiO₂. Please also include the spectrum of TiO₂ to enable comparison of the OH region. Use the same enlarged view and scaling of the OH region in Fig. S24a and Fig. S24b to allow a direct comparison.
14. The authors state in line 157 that “[Cu–O] sites effectively suppress side reactions, including alkene hydrogenation and over-dehydrogenation.” This conclusion is not supported by comparative data. There is no direct comparison with TiO₂ or other controls that would demonstrate suppression rather than simply low intrinsic activity under the tested conditions. In addition, C₂H₆ is detected in reactions 2, 3, and 4, which indicates some hydrogenation occurs. Figure S8 supports only that Cu/TiO₂ is not efficient for C₂H₄ and C₂H₂ hydrogenation under the specific test conditions. Please provide additional evidence clarifying the role of Cu in the reaction and the role of CO₂.
15. Figure S9A does not show a dark control at an equivalent catalyst surface temperature.
16. How do C₁₀H₁₀Fe, K₂S₂O₈, (NH₄)₂C₂O₄, and NH₃ affect the surface properties, including the Cu valence and C₂H₆ adsorption? How to rule out residual effects of these reagents on the surface as a cause of the reduced activity?
17. The way the ethyl is coordinated to the surface as shown in the *C2H5+*H panel in Fig. 5c seems odd for an intermediate (unless it’s a transition state), since based on coordination chemistry principles one would expect coordination through the carbon – is there experimental evidence supporting H-coordination to the surface?
18. For Fig. 5c, what does each of the paths mean, and why do paths 1 and 2 become disconnected? I would avoid using percentages when comparing two different energies since it may be misleading and at times confusing to the reader (i.e. the 96.6% has a smaller gap than the 62.3%) but instead report the energy difference directly.
19. For the computational methods, a +U correction is typically not applied to the oxygen but only the metal – if there’s any special reason for this it should be discussed; for the Ti, why was 4.2 eV chosen (is there a reference to it an experimental/computational benchmark?)
20. The authors report delta G values and provide the equation associated with it, but there was no mention of how the entropy was obtained (i.e. were any vibrational/phonon calculations done, and how are the associated contributions to the vibrational part of the entropy obtained?)
21. For the TS search, how the constrained optimization technique was used should be discussed.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This manuscript by Lingzhi Wang and coworkers reported a site-defined photocatalytic strategy for the selective light-driven dehydrogenation of ethane (C₂H₆) to ethylene (C₂H₄) using atomically dispersed Cu–O ensembles on TiO₂ (Cu₁/TiO₂). The study highlights that Cu atoms coordinated with bridging oxygen form well-defined [Cu–O] motifs, which serve as active centers for stepwise C–H activation and H₂ evolution. Photogenerated holes localize at Obr–Cu sites to initiate the first C–H cleavage, while adjacent Cu centers mediate β–H elimination, resulting in efficient and hydrogen-conserving C₂H₆ upgrading. This catalyst achieved an impressive C₂H₄ yield of 21.1 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹, 97% C₂H₄ selectivity, and a quantum efficiency of 6.1% at 365 nm, outperforming state-of-the-art photocatalytic ethane dehydrogenation systems. The co-feeding of CO₂ was found to selectively scavenge surface *H species, thereby preventing catalyst deactivation and preserving long-term activity. The mechanism is well-supported by a combination of in situ EPR, DRIFTS, NAP-XPS, TRFL, fs-TAS, and DFT calculations, which collectively reveal that [Cu–O] ensembles orchestrate cooperative charge transfer and redox functionality, enabling controlled C–H activation and H₂ evolution under mild conditions. This paper provides atomic-level insight into the design of redox-cooperative single-atom photocatalysts for alkane upgrading and contributes significantly to the development of sustainable, low-temperature C–H activation chemistry. This paper will be potentially acceptable for publication in Nature Communications. However, I do not recommend publication in the present form because some questions need to be answered.
1. The authors' characterization (XPS, XAS) clearly indicates that the as-prepared catalyst contains a substantial fraction of Cu+ (approx. 38% based on XPS deconvolution), coexisting with Cu2+. The manuscript's mechanistic discussion, however, focuses almost exclusively on the role of the [Cu2+−O 4] motif as the primary active site for C-H activation and H₂ evolution. The role of the significant initial population of [Cu+−O3] sites remains ambiguous. Are the Cu+ sites catalytically active for any step of the reaction, or are they merely spectators? Can these sites act as electron traps or play another role in the charge carrier dynamics that influence the overall efficiency? Is there any evidence for the interconversion between Cu+ and Cu2+ under reaction conditions, beyond the deactivation pathway identified?
2. The authors report a catalyst surface temperature of ~108 °C under illumination. While the control experiments (wavelength dependence, dark controls, and a significantly lower activation energy under light) provide strong evidence for a predominantly photocatalytic mechanism, the potential contribution of a photothermal effect at this temperature warrants a more detailed discussion. A localized thermal effect could still play a role in overcoming certain reaction barriers. The authors should provide a more quantitative analysis or discussion to deconvolve the quantum effects from the light-induced thermal effects to strengthen their mechanistic claims further.
3. The strategy of using CO2 to regenerate the catalyst by scavenging poisonous *H species is a highlight of this work. However, this process produces CO as a byproduct. The 20-hour stability test is promising, but for potential practical applications, the long-term consequences should be considered. Can the accumulation of CO in a continuous or recycle reactor lead to catalyst poisoning (e.g., via carbonyl formation on Cu sites) or promote side reactions like the reverse water-gas shift reaction with the co-produced H2?
4. In the abstract, the phrase "adjacent Cu centers mediate -H elimination" should be specified as "β-H elimination" for clarity, consistent with the terminology used later in the manuscript.
5. The observation that C4H10 is formed when Cu sites are blocked by NH3 is interesting. The authors state that this is because ∙CH5 radicals prefer coupling. A brief mechanistic explanation would be beneficial, clarifying why this occurs (e.g., due to increased surface concentration and lifetime of the radicals in the absence of a site for the second dehydrogenation step).
6. The photocatalytic process is modeled under excited-state conditions, but the manuscript does not fully clarify how the "excited" surface states are constructed in DFT. Are the results from constrained hole localization sufficient to capture the photogenerated carrier distribution? A more detailed explanation of how the excited-state pathway is modeled would be better.
7. The reported barrier for C–H activation at Obr–Cu under photoexcited conditions (0.46 eV) is impressively low compared to thermal activation (0.46 vs 1.2 eV+). However, the paper would benefit from additional comparison across different sites (Obr–Cu vs Obr–Ti vs terrace Ti sites) under the same computational framework, to confirm the relative preference quantitatively.
8. The calculated barriers for *H migration (2.9–3.1 eV) are high, supporting the conclusion of *H accumulation. However, the authors could further discuss whether such high-energy events are still feasible under photon-driven conditions (where local hot carriers may contribute). The neglect of non-adiabatic effects may lead to an underestimation of possible *H dynamics.
9. The proposed *H scavenging pathway via CO₂ → *HCOO → CO is strongly supported by DRIFTS and isotope labeling, but the DFT section only briefly covers CO₂ reactivity. It would strengthen the work if the energy profile for *HCOO formation and decomposition were presented explicitly, in parallel with the C₂H₆ dehydrogenation pathway.
10. Following the first question, the experimental results show that the catalyst contains a significant amount of Cu+ (~38%). The current DFT model in Figure 5C focuses on what appears to be a Cu2+ site. Given the prevalence of Cu+, its potential role in the catalytic cycle cannot be ignored. Did the authors perform calculations on a model containing a Cu+ site (e.g., a [Cu+−O3] unit)? A comparative calculation of the C-H activation barrier on a modeled Cu+ site would be highly insightful. If the barrier is significantly higher, it would strengthen the claim that Cu2+ is the primary active state. If the barrier is comparable, it would suggest a more complex picture.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their time and effort in evaluating our manuscript entitled "Site-defined Cu-O ensembles enable hydrogen-conserving light-driven ethane upgrading" (Manuscript Number: NCOMMS-25-73862-T). We are truly grateful for your constructive comments, which not only guide our research but also greatly help improve the manuscript quality. All comments have been carefully considered, and additional experiments have been performed where appropriate. Point-by-point responses are provided below, and the corresponding revisions have been incorporated into the revised manuscript. For clarity, reviewer comments are shown in blue, our responses in black, and changes in the manuscript are highlighted in yellow.
Response to Reviewer #1
General Comment: In this manuscript, the authors reported an investigation of synthesis of single atom Cu-loaded on TiO for photocatalytic ethane dehydrogenation with or without CO . In the work, the authors carried out a comprehensive investigation on the catalytic performance and mechanism. From the experimental tests and DFT calculation, the authors have presented a clear mechanism on the photocatalysis. The work is innovation and provide new information on the catalytic system. It can be published after revision.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your positive assessment of our work as well as your encouraging and valuable comments. We have carefully considered all of your comments and provide detailed, point-by-point responses below.
Comment 1: The authors prepared several different metal-loaded catalysts and found that these catalysts presented various activity. However, they did not discuss the underline reason. It would be better for the authors to check if all the catalysts are single-atom catalysts.
Response: We sincerely appreciate you for your valuable suggestions, which have significantly contributed to validating the reliability and universality of the single-atom catalyst synthesis method employed in our work. We fully understand the concern about confirming the structural characteristics of each metal catalyst. It should be emphasized that all metal loaded catalysts in this study were prepared using exactly the same synthetic protocol, in which key parameters such as precursor concentration, loading procedure, and calcination conditions were strictly kept identical. Therefore, taking comprehensive considerations into account, we selected Ag/TiO catalyst as a representative to supplement HAADF-STEM and EXAFS characterizations for further verifying the universality of the synthesis method. Isolated atomic bright spots of Ag species are observed in HAADF-STEM images, and EXAFS spectra show only Ag-O signals with no signals corresponding to Ag-Ag bonds or Ag-(O)-Ag bonds, clearly confirming that Ag is dispersed as single atoms (please see renumbered Supplementary Fig. 6). Together with the previously confirmed single-atom nature of Cu /TiO , these results strongly support the universality of this synthesis method in preparing single-atom active centers.
Furthermore, we would like to clarify that the primary scientific objective of this work is to elucidate the reaction mechanism of Cu /TiO . The data for other metal single-atom catalysts are included mainly to place the performance of Cu /TiO in a broader catalytic context, rather than to provide a systematic, metal-by-metal interpretation of activity differences. The observed variations in activity are likely governed by a complex interplay of factors, including electronic structure, metal–support interaction strength, and the adsorption energetics of key reaction intermediates. A rigorous, quantitative analysis of these multidimensional structure–activity correlations would require a dedicated, systematic study and therefore lies beyond the scope of the present manuscript. We fully agree that this is an important topic and have identified it as a promising direction for future work, in which we plan to carry out comprehensive comparative investigations across different metal single-atom catalysts.
The characterization data for Ag/TiO and related discussions have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 5, first paragraph), further strengthening the evidence for the generality of the synthesis method.

Response: We sincerely thank you for raising this critical question regarding the catalytic roles of the two distinct copper species, [Cu–O ] and [Cu–O ], in the Cu /TiO catalyst. Our comprehensive analysis integrating in situ spectroscopic characterization with first-principles calculations unequivocally identifies the [Cu–O ] motif being identified as the primary active center for non-oxidative ethane dehydrogenation. This conclusion is robustly supported by quasi-in situ EPR (renumbered Supplementary Fig. 11) and in situ NAP-XPS (Figs. 5a and 5b) analyses, which consistently show that catalyst deactivation process is always accompanied by a pronounced decrease in the Cu2+ signal (associated with the [Cu–O ] motif). To further clarify the role of [Cu–O ] and strengthen the assignment of [Cu–O ] as the main active site, we performed additional DFT calculations comparing β–H activation of the ·C H intermediate on these two motifs, guided by the active-species quenching experiments in Fig. 4b, which indicate that Cu sites are responsible for β–H activation. The results (please see renumbered Supplementary Fig. 32) reveal that on the most representative [Cu–O ] motif, the reaction energy for β–H bond cleavage in the ·C H intermediate is as high as 1.06 eV, indicating a strongly endergonic process. In sharp contrast, the same C–H activation step on the [Cu–O ] motif exhibits a much lower reaction energy of only 0.11 eV. This pronounced energy difference clearly demonstrates that [Cu–O ] ensembles as the key active centers for β–H activation, whereas [Cu–O ] ensembles make only a minor contribution to this crucial step.
Admittedly, due to the objective limitations of catalyst synthesis methods and the complexity of Cu valence state regulation, the existence of the [Cu–O ] structure is an intrinsic characteristic of the current system. Nevertheless, its presence does not affect the identification of the main active site. To further clarify the conclusion regarding [Cu–O ] as the primary active center, relevant insights have been comprehensively incorporated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 12, second paragraph), offering a more rigorous and coherent mechanistic explanation for the structure-activity relationship of the catalytic system.

As outlined in the manuscript, the *H generated from β–H desorption at the O site does not readily desorb as H due to the high barrier of H–H coupling, leading to the deactivation of [Cu–O ] sites via *H coverage. It should be noted that this dehydration step is still thermodynamically endergonic. Under CO co‑feeding, CO cooperates with ·C H radicals from other sites to restore the [Cu–O ] structure via the *COOH pathway. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 37, adsorbed CO abstracts a β–H from ·C H to form *COOH (barrier: 1.32 eV), which then readily decomposes to adsorbed CO (barrier: 0.04 eV). After CO desorption, the [Cu–O ] site is regenerated and can continue to participate in β–H elimination, with the released *H subsequently coupling to form H . By contrast, direct CO dissociation via the MvK mechanism requires overcoming a much higher activation barrier (1.96 eV) and reaction energy (1.85 eV) (see Response Fig. R1), further corroborating the relative feasibility of the aforementioned cooperative pathway. These findings have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 13, first paragraph), and we appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments.

Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful comments, which have provided important guidance for improving our experimental design and data presentation. In accordance with your suggestions, we have revised the manuscript and supplemented the relevant descriptions as follows.
First, regarding your concern that the time evolution of pressure in the sealed batch reactor may influence the apparent activity, we have added in situ records of the pressure difference, defined as the difference between the instantaneous pressure and the initial pressure, as a function of time, as well as the catalyst surface temperature as a function of time, under a reaction atmosphere of 20 vol% C H /20 vol% CO /Ar (please see renumbered Supplementary Fig. 12). In these experiments, the initial pressure in the reactor was 1.0 atm, and a AS511A digital differential manometer (SMART SENSOR) was used to continuously monitor the pressure during the reaction. The results show that, immediately after the introduction of light irradiation, the system pressure increases rapidly, which can be mainly attributed to enhanced gas molecular motion induced by the photothermal effect. This was followed by a slow and nearly linear pressure increase, corresponding to the ongoing C H dehydrogenation reaction. It is important to emphasize that throughout the entire reaction process, the maximum pressure increase is less than 10 kPa, which is below 10% of the initial pressure. Therefore, we consider that the pressure variation within this range has a negligible influence on the reaction rate and the evaluation of apparent activity and does not compromise the reliability of the conclusions. The descriptions of relevant data and corresponding measurement methods have been clearly integrated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 7, second paragraph and page 14, “Batch-type performance test” section).
Second, regarding the measurement of the catalyst surface temperature and the procedure for setting and calibrating the emissivity (ε), we have provided a detailed description in the “Methods” section of the revised manuscript. Specifically, the catalyst surface temperature was mainly monitored using a Uti160S infrared thermal imager (UNI-T). During the experiments, the camera was fixed at an oblique angle above the reactor and focused on the top surface of the catalyst bed in order to acquire thermal images of the catalyst layer. The emissivity of the camera was set to ε = 0.95. This value was obtained through an empirical calibration procedure in which a thin, uniformly spread layer of catalyst powder was placed at the center of a pre-calibrated heating plate. The temperature of the heating plate was successively set to 50, 100, 150, and 200°C, and the emissivity parameter of the thermal imager was adjusted until the infrared readings of the catalyst surface at each temperature matched the actual temperature of the heating plate as closely as possible. The resulting emissivity value was then used in all subsequent temperature measurements. In addition, to further verify the accuracy of the temperature measurements, we simultaneously recorded the catalyst surface temperature as a function of time using a K-type thermocouple under identical reaction conditions, as shown in renumbered Supplementary Fig. 12. The temperatures obtained from the thermocouple show excellent agreement with those measured by the infrared thermal camera, which provides additional confirmation of the reliability of the temperature measurement method. The complete calibration procedure of the thermal imager and the detailed protocol for surface temperature measurement have been systematically added to the “Methods” section of the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 14, “Batch-type performance test” section).
We again sincerely thank you for your careful review and valuable comments, which have significantly improved the completeness and transparency of the manuscript with respect to the description of experimental methods and the rigor of the data.

Response: We thank you for your careful comments. We have corrected the spelling error of "Yield" and conducted a systematic check of the entire manuscript to ensure no similar issues remain.
Regarding the apparent contradiction between the C H yield under high light intensity (310 mW cm-2) in Fig. S9B (now renumbered Supplementary Fig. 10b) and the result under lower intensity in Supplementary Table 2 stems from the intrinsic difference between the light sources. As confirmed by the control experiments in Fig. S9C (now renumbered Supplementary Fig. 10c), the catalyst activity is mainly derived from the ultraviolet region, as this range can effectively excite the TiO . In the AQY test (Supplementary Table 2), a 365 nm monochromatic light source was used, which matches the catalyst's optimal absorption. This ensures highly efficient photon usage and a high quantum yield. By contrast, the test for Fig. S9B used a full-spectrum Xenon lamp (250~1100 nm, see spectral profile in Fig. R1 below). Although the total irradiance is higher, the spectrum contains a large fraction of visible and infrared light, to which the catalyst responds poorly. Therefore, the flux of effective UV photons under the full-spectrum 310 mW cm-2 condition is much lower than under the 54 mW cm-2 monochromatic light.
