## Methods

Preparation of catalysts
Synthesis of MIL-125(Tiv). The MIL-125 with Ti vacancies (Ti v ) precursor was synthesized according to the method described in previous literature41. First, 3.0 g of terephthalic acid (99%, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) was dissolved in 54 mL of N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 99.9%, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) with 30 min magnetic stirring at room temperature. Subsequently, 6 mL of methanol (99.9%, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) was added and stirred for 5 min, followed by the addition of 1.2 mL of tetrabutyl titanate (TBOT, 99%, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) with additional 5 min stirring. The mixture was transferred to a sealed round-bottom flask and reacted at 130 °C for 20 h under Ar atmosphere using an oil bath. After cooling, the precipitate was collected by centrifugation, successively washed twice with DMF and twice with methanol, and vacuum-dried at 80 °C for 10 h to remove residual solvents, yielding MIL-125(Tiv).

Synthesis of Cu /TiO . 150 mg of MIL-125(Tiv) was dispersed in 50 mL of water/methanol solution (1:4 v/v). Under continuous stirring, a predetermined aliquot of 0.1 M CuCl (99.99%, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) aqueous solution was added dropwise, followed by stirring for 10 h. The resulting mixture was centrifuged and washed thrice with water/methanol solution. After oven-drying at 80 °C, the solid was calcined in a muffle furnace at 500 °C for 4 h with a heating rate of 2 °C/min to obtain Cu /TiO .

Evaluation of catalytic performance
Batch-type performance test. First, the catalyst was uniformly dispersed in 1.0 mL deionized water and coated onto a glass slide (coating area: 3.14 cm2), followed by drying at 80 °C. The catalyst-coated glass slide was placed at the center of the bottom of a sealed 100 mL quartz reactor. To ensure complete replacement of residual air by ethane, the reactor was subjected to three evacuation/ethane-flushing cycles (1 atm, 99.9% C H per cycle) before performance test. A 300 W full-spectrum (250 ~1100 nm) Xe lamp (PLS-SXE300+) was used for vertical irradiation (4 h per reaction) without additional external heating, and the light intensity was monitored using a PL-MW2000 optical power meter. Pressure changes (defined as the difference between the instantaneous pressure and the initial pressure) during the reaction were continuously recorded with an AS511A digital differential manometer (SMART SENSOR). The reaction products were analyzed using a Shimadzu gas chromatograph (GC-2014C) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionization detector (FID). For the C18O 2 isotope-labeled experiment, the gas-phase products were detected by a 7890A-5975C gas chromatography-mass spectrometer (Agilent Technologies Co., Ltd.).

The catalyst surface temperature was simultaneously monitored using a Uti160S infrared thermal imager (UNI-T) and a calibrated K-type thermocouple (diameter 0.25 mm, KAIPUSEN). The thermocouple probe maintained direct contact with the center of the catalyst bed, while the thermal imager was installed at an oblique angle above the reactor, oriented toward the top surface of the catalyst bed to capture thermal image data. The emissivity was established as ε = 0.95 based on an empirical calibration procedure performed with catalyst powder distributed uniformly on a pre-calibrated heating plate. During calibration, the heating plate temperature was systematically varied (50, 100, 150, and 200 °C) and the imager's emissivity setting was adjusted until its temperature readings concurred with the reference values at each point, thereby determining the optimal emissivity value for all subsequent experimental measurements.

Flow-type performance test. The performance tests of flow-type PEDH and TEDH were both evaluated in a PLS-LED 100 photothermal reactor (Beijing Perfectlight) equipped with external temperature control, where the catalyst-bed temperature was monitored by a KE-type thermocouple inserted into the center of the catalyst layer. For each test, 10 mg of catalyst was uniformly coated onto a heat-resistant quartz fiber filter membrane (fixed coating area: 3.14 cm2), and the flow rate of the feed gas (20 vol% C H /20 vol% CO /Ar) was set as 10 mL min-1. The apparent activation energy measurements were carried out in the same reactor, in which a UV light source with fixed intensity was employed to mitigate photothermal effects, and a relatively low temperature window of 60~140 ℃ was selected to ensure that the reaction proceeded in the kinetic regime and to minimize interference from internal and external mass transfer and thermal effects.

The corresponding product yield, selectivity, conversion, and carbon balance were calculated using the following equations:
Yield = [C H ] / (m*t) [1]
Selectivity = [C H ] / ([C H ]+0.5*[CH ]+2*[C H ]) *100% [2]
Conversion = ([C H ] - [C H ]) / [C H ] *100% [3]
Carbon balance = ([C H ]+0.5*[CH ]+2*[C H ]) / [C H ] [4]
where [C H ], [CH ], [C H ] and [C H ] represent the molar amounts of C H , CH , C H and C H , respectively. m and t represent the mass of the catalyst (g) and the reaction time (h), respectively.

Characterization
The morphological characteristics of the samples were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Helios G4 UC), transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Talos F200X), and aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM, Themis Z). Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were acquired using a Rigaku D/MAX 2550 diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.5406 Å), scanning the 2θ range from 5° to 80° at a rate of 8° min-1. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was performed using an ESCALAB 250Xi system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with monochromatic Al Kα radiation (hν=1486.6 eV), and the binding energies were referenced and corrected using the C 1s peak at 284.8 eV. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) measurements were conducted on an Agilent 5800 VDV system. Thermogravimetric/differential thermal analysis (TG/DTA) was conducted using a Netzsch TGA209F1 instrument, with the temperature ranging from 50 to 800 °C. Raman spectroscopy measurements were performed using a Renishaw inVia Raman system, with a 532 nm laser serving as the excitation source. UV-Vis diffuse reflectance spectra of the dry-pressed disk samples were recorded on a Cary 500 spectrophotometer (Varian) with an integrating sphere, using BaSO as a reflectance reference standard. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements were performed using a 100G-18KG/EMX-8/2.7 instrument. Transient photocurrent response and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were conducted using a ZAHNER PP211 electrochemical workstation with a standard three-electrode configuration. The working electrode consisted of fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) glass coated with the sample (5 mg, coating area: 1 cm2), with a platinum counter electrode and a saturated calomel electrode as a reference electrode. Transient photocurrent tests were performed in 0.5 M aqueous Na SO solution, while EIS measurements were carried out in an electrolyte system containing potassium ferricyanide. Ammonia temperature-programmed desorption (NH -TPD) measurements were performed on a Micromeritics AutoChem II 2920 chemisorption analyzer. Following saturation with 10% NH /He gas mixture at 50 °C, the sample was heated from 50 to 800 °C at a rate of 10 °C min-1 under a He flow, while the desorbed gases were monitored via a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). C H -TPD measurements followed an identical procedure to that of NH -TPD, with catalyst saturation achieved via pulsed injection of pure C H gas into the system. Temperature-programmed surface reaction (TPSR) experiments were performed on a TP5080 automatic multi-purpose adsorption analyzer, and the desorbed products were monitored in situ using a Hiden Analytical DECAR mass spectrometer during linear heating from 50 to 800 °C at 10 °C min-1. For C H -TPSR, the feed gas consisted of 20% C H balanced with Ar; for C H /CO -TPSR, the feed gas was composed of 20 vol% C H /20 vol% CO balanced with Ar.

XAFS measurement
Cu K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) was collected in fluorescence mode at the XAFCA beamline of the Singapore Synchrotron Light Source (SSLS). Measurements employed a double-crystal Si (111) monochromator with energy calibration referenced to a Cu foil. O K-edge XAFS measurements were performed at the soft X-ray beamline of the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) (Hefei, China). The XAS data were processed using the Demeter software package (ATHENA and ARTEMIS)59.

In situ experiments
In situ synchrotron-based vacuum ultraviolet-photoionization mass spectrometry (SVUV-PIMS). In situ SVUV-PIMS measurements were conducted at the Atomic and Molecular Physics beamline (BL09U) in the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) (Hefei, China)60. The catalyst was positioned at the center of a laminar flow reactor cell. Reaction products were sampled via molecular beam into the ionization chamber, ionized by synchrotron VUV light, and detected by a time-of-flight mass spectrometer. The experiment began by purging the reaction cell’s differential chamber (pressure stabilized at 20.0 Pa) with 50 vol% C H /Ar at a flow rate of 20 mL min-1 for 30 min to remove air. Illumination was provided by a 300 W xenon lamp (without external heating). Following 30 min of illumination, mass spectra were acquired at 10.5 eV with an integration time of 1000 s. Product photoionization efficiency (PIE) curves were scanned from 8.0 to 11.5 eV with an integration time of 240 s per point. The same procedure was repeated for data collection after switching the feed gas to 50 vol% C H /CO mixture.

In situ femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (fs-TAS). In situ fs-TAS measurements were performed using a Helios spectrometer (Ultrafast system) under pure Ar, 50 vol% C H /Ar, or 50 vol% C H /50 vol%CO . The amplified femtosecond Ti: sapphire laser system operated at a repetition rate of 1 kHz, and the probe light was collected via the lens of an InGaAs diode array.

In-situ time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy (TRFL). In situ TRFL spectra were acquired on an Edinburgh Instruments FLS 980 spectrometer. Samples were sealed in 1 mm-pathlength quartz microcuvettes and measured under pure Ar, C H , or CO atmosphere. Excitation was provided by a 360 nm light-emitting diode (LED) source.

In situ NAP-XPS. In situ NAP-XPS was performed on a Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi system with Al Kα radiation (hν = 1486.6 eV). After Ar⁺ sputtering (3 keV, 40 eV pass energy, 0.1 eV step, 1 min), XPS data under vacuum were first collected, after which 50 vol% C H /Ar or 50 vol% C H /50 vol% CO were continuously introduced. Spectra were recorded sequentially under dark conditions, as well as 20 and 40 min after illumination with a 300 W xenon lamp. NAP-XPS spectra were averaged over 5 scans with charge referencing to C 1s (284.80 eV).

In situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS). In situ DRIFTS measurements were performed on a Thermo Fisher-Nicolet iS20 infrared spectrometer equipped with a liquid nitrogen-cooled mercury-cadmium-telluride (MCT) detector, using a three-window diffuse-reflectance cell (Harrick). Before the test, samples were dehydrated at 120 °C for 1 h. Subsequently, 0.1 g of the dried catalyst was loaded into the sample cell and purged with Ar (99.9 vol%) for 30 min to eliminate surface-adsorbed species. Following Ar purging, a background spectrum was collected under an Ar atmosphere. Ar was then flushed out, and a continuous flow of reactant gas (either 20 vol% C H /Ar or 20 vol% C H /20 vol% CO /Ar) was introduced at a flow rate of 20 mL min-1. Spectra were collected at specified time intervals after initiating light irradiation. The spectral resolution was 4 cm-1, and the scanning range was 4000–600 cm-1.

Theoretical calculations
All spin-polarized calculations were performed with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional within the generalized gradient approximation using the VASP 6.3.2 code61,62. The valence electronic states were expanded in plane-wave basis sets with an energy cutoff at 450 eV, and the occupancy of the one-electron states was calculated using the Gaussian smearing with SIGMA = 0.05 eV. The on-site Hubbard U term (PBE+U) was added for O orbitals and Ti orbitals with a value of 4.0 eV and 4.2 eV to facilitate the localization of trapped holes and electrons. In particular, the U correction on the O 2p orbitals helps to cancel self-interaction errors and enables a more realistic localization of photogenerated holes on surface O sites. In addition, to simplify the treatment of the photoexcited system by excluding the uncertain electron–hole interactions that depend on the specific trapping center, while simultaneously preserving the charge neutrality of the periodic slab and avoiding artificial background-charge corrections, an -OH group was introduced on the bottom surface as an electron acceptor63. To validate the accuracy of the DFT+U method64, complementary HSE06 hybrid functional calculations were systematically performed for all reaction steps, with corresponding energy values exclusively derived from the HSE0627. Structure optimizations were performed using the Quasi-Newton Broyden minimization scheme until the atomic forces on each ion were less than 0.05 eV/Å. The transition states (TSs) were searched using a constrained optimization scheme65. In this approach, we keep the C–H bond distance fixed at preselected values, and minimize the total energy with respect to all remaining orthogonal degrees of freedom. In practice, this allows the adsorbed molecules to rotate and translate under the imposed constraint, and the TiO surface is fully relaxed. A transition state is identified when the forces on all atoms vanish and the total energy exhibits a maximum along the chosen reaction coordinate while remaining a minimum with respect to all other degrees of freedom.

A 4-layer p (2×3) unit cell of 10.3 Å, 11.4 Å with a 20.0 Å vacuum between the slabs in the z direction was used for the construction of the anatase TiO (101) surface. The Brillouin zone was sampled with a 3×2×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh. The free energy calculations are based on Eq.5: ΔG=ΔE+ΔZPE-ΔTS [5] where E is the calculated total energy of the model, ZPE is the change of zero-point vibrational enthalpy, and TS is the entropy. For adsorbed intermediates, vibrational frequencies were calculated at the optimized geometries and used to obtain ΔZPE and the vibrational contribution to ΔS at 383 K. The ΔG corrections were then evaluated using the VASPKIT post-processing tool based on these vibrational frequencies66. For gas-phase species, translational, rotational and vibrational entropy contributions at 383 K were taken from standard thermochemical data (NIST).

At first glance, the work appears to deliver a major advance in activity; however, the activity is overstated and the interpretation is not sufficiently critical. ### Reviewer 4

This manuscript by Lingzhi Wang and coworkers reported a site-defined photocatalytic strategy for the selective light-driven dehydrogenation of ethane (C₂H₆) to ethylene (C₂H₄) using atomically dispersed Cu–O ensembles on TiO₂ (Cu₁/TiO₂). The study highlights that Cu atoms coordinated with bridging oxygen form well-defined [Cu–O] motifs, which serve as active centers for stepwise C–H activation and H₂ evolution. Photogenerated holes localize at Obr–Cu sites to initiate the first C–H cleavage, while adjacent Cu centers mediate β–H elimination, resulting in efficient and hydrogen-conserving C₂H₆ upgrading. This catalyst achieved an impressive C₂H₄ yield of 21.1 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹, 97% C₂H₄ selectivity, and a quantum efficiency of 6.1% at 365 nm, outperforming state-of-the-art photocatalytic ethane dehydrogenation systems. The co-feeding of CO₂ was found to selectively scavenge surface *H species, thereby preventing catalyst deactivation and preserving long-term activity. The mechanism is well-supported by a combination of in situ EPR, DRIFTS, NAP-XPS, TRFL, fs-TAS, and DFT calculations, which collectively reveal that [Cu–O] ensembles orchestrate cooperative charge transfer and redox functionality, enabling controlled C–H activation and H₂ evolution under mild conditions. This paper provides atomic-level insight into the design of redox-cooperative single-atom photocatalysts for alkane upgrading and contributes significantly to the development of sustainable, low-temperature C–H activation chemistry. This paper will be potentially acceptable for publication in Nature Communications. However, I do not recommend publication in the present form because some questions need to be answered.
1. The authors' characterization (XPS, XAS) clearly indicates that the as-prepared catalyst contains a substantial fraction of Cu+ (approx. 38% based on XPS deconvolution), coexisting with Cu2+. The manuscript's mechanistic discussion, however, focuses almost exclusively on the role of the [Cu2+−O 4] motif as the primary active site for C-H activation and H₂ evolution. The role of the significant initial population of [Cu+−O3] sites remains ambiguous. Are the Cu+ sites catalytically active for any step of the reaction, or are they merely spectators? Can these sites act as electron traps or play another role in the charge carrier dynamics that influence the overall efficiency? Is there any evidence for the interconversion between Cu+ and Cu2+ under reaction conditions, beyond the deactivation pathway identified?
2. The authors report a catalyst surface temperature of ~108 °C under illumination. While the control experiments (wavelength dependence, dark controls, and a significantly lower activation energy under light) provide strong evidence for a predominantly photocatalytic mechanism, the potential contribution of a photothermal effect at this temperature warrants a more detailed discussion. A localized thermal effect could still play a role in overcoming certain reaction barriers. The authors should provide a more quantitative analysis or discussion to deconvolve the quantum effects from the light-induced thermal effects to strengthen their mechanistic claims further.
3. The strategy of using CO2 to regenerate the catalyst by scavenging poisonous *H species is a highlight of this work. However, this process produces CO as a byproduct. The 20-hour stability test is promising, but for potential practical applications, the long-term consequences should be considered. Can the accumulation of CO in a continuous or recycle reactor lead to catalyst poisoning (e.g., via carbonyl formation on Cu sites) or promote side reactions like the reverse water-gas shift reaction with the co-produced H2?
4. In the abstract, the phrase "adjacent Cu centers mediate -H elimination" should be specified as "β-H elimination" for clarity, consistent with the terminology used later in the manuscript.
5. The observation that C4H10 is formed when Cu sites are blocked by NH3 is interesting. The authors state that this is because ∙CH5 radicals prefer coupling. A brief mechanistic explanation would be beneficial, clarifying why this occurs (e.g., due to increased surface concentration and lifetime of the radicals in the absence of a site for the second dehydrogenation step).
6. The photocatalytic process is modeled under excited-state conditions, but the manuscript does not fully clarify how the "excited" surface states are constructed in DFT. Are the results from constrained hole localization sufficient to capture the photogenerated carrier distribution? A more detailed explanation of how the excited-state pathway is modeled would be better.
7. The reported barrier for C–H activation at Obr–Cu under photoexcited conditions (0.46 eV) is impressively low compared to thermal activation (0.46 vs 1.2 eV+). However, the paper would benefit from additional comparison across different sites (Obr–Cu vs Obr–Ti vs terrace Ti sites) under the same computational framework, to confirm the relative preference quantitatively.
8. The calculated barriers for *H migration (2.9–3.1 eV) are high, supporting the conclusion of *H accumulation. However, the authors could further discuss whether such high-energy events are still feasible under photon-driven conditions (where local hot carriers may contribute). The neglect of non-adiabatic effects may lead to an underestimation of possible *H dynamics.
9. The proposed *H scavenging pathway via CO₂ → *HCOO → CO is strongly supported by DRIFTS and isotope labeling, but the DFT section only briefly covers CO₂ reactivity. It would strengthen the work if the energy profile for *HCOO formation and decomposition were presented explicitly, in parallel with the C₂H₆ dehydrogenation pathway.
10. Following the first question, the experimental results show that the catalyst contains a significant amount of Cu+ (~38%). The current DFT model in Figure 5C focuses on what appears to be a Cu2+ site. Given the prevalence of Cu+, its potential role in the catalytic cycle cannot be ignored. Did the authors perform calculations on a model containing a Cu+ site (e.g., a [Cu+−O3] unit)? A comparative calculation of the C-H activation barrier on a modeled Cu+ site would be highly insightful. If the barrier is significantly higher, it would strengthen the claim that Cu2+ is the primary active state. If the barrier is comparable, it would suggest a more complex picture.

Response to Reviewer #1
General Comment: In this manuscript, the authors reported an investigation of synthesis of single atom Cu-loaded on TiO for photocatalytic ethane dehydrogenation with or without CO . In the work, the authors carried out a comprehensive investigation on the catalytic performance and mechanism. From the experimental tests and DFT calculation, the authors have presented a clear mechanism on the photocatalysis. The work is innovation and provide new information on the catalytic system. It can be published after revision.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your positive assessment of our work as well as your encouraging and valuable comments. We have carefully considered all of your comments and provide detailed, point-by-point responses below.
Comment 1: The authors prepared several different metal-loaded catalysts and found that these catalysts presented various activity. However, they did not discuss the underline reason. It would be better for the authors to check if all the catalysts are single-atom catalysts.
Response: We sincerely appreciate you for your valuable suggestions, which have significantly contributed to validating the reliability and universality of the single-atom catalyst synthesis method employed in our work. We fully understand the concern about confirming the structural characteristics of each metal catalyst. It should be emphasized that all metal loaded catalysts in this study were prepared using exactly the same synthetic protocol, in which key parameters such as precursor concentration, loading procedure, and calcination conditions were strictly kept identical. Therefore, taking comprehensive considerations into account, we selected Ag/TiO catalyst as a representative to supplement HAADF-STEM and EXAFS characterizations for further verifying the universality of the synthesis method. Isolated atomic bright spots of Ag species are observed in HAADF-STEM images, and EXAFS spectra show only Ag-O signals with no signals corresponding to Ag-Ag bonds or Ag-(O)-Ag bonds, clearly confirming that Ag is dispersed as single atoms (please see renumbered Supplementary Fig. 6). Together with the previously confirmed single-atom nature of Cu /TiO , these results strongly support the universality of this synthesis method in preparing single-atom active centers.
Furthermore, we would like to clarify that the primary scientific objective of this work is to elucidate the reaction mechanism of Cu /TiO . The data for other metal single-atom catalysts are included mainly to place the performance of Cu /TiO in a broader catalytic context, rather than to provide a systematic, metal-by-metal interpretation of activity differences. The observed variations in activity are likely governed by a complex interplay of factors, including electronic structure, metal–support interaction strength, and the adsorption energetics of key reaction intermediates. A rigorous, quantitative analysis of these multidimensional structure–activity correlations would require a dedicated, systematic study and therefore lies beyond the scope of the present manuscript. We fully agree that this is an important topic and have identified it as a promising direction for future work, in which we plan to carry out comprehensive comparative investigations across different metal single-atom catalysts.
The characterization data for Ag/TiO and related discussions have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 5, first paragraph), further strengthening the evidence for the generality of the synthesis method.

Taken together, we assign [Cu–O ] as the predominant configuration for Cu2+ species, while [Cu–O ] corresponds to Cu+ sites. To further evaluate the generality of this MOF-based pre-encapsulation strategy for synthesizing single-atom catalysts, we additionally prepared Ag/TiO under identical synthetic conditions. Comment 2: In the work, the authors suggested two Cu species in Cu /TiO , Cu-O and Cu-O . What are the detailed roles of these species in catalysis?
Response: We sincerely thank you for raising this critical question regarding the catalytic roles of the two distinct copper species, [Cu–O ] and [Cu–O ], in the Cu /TiO catalyst. Our comprehensive analysis integrating in situ spectroscopic characterization with first-principles calculations unequivocally identifies the [Cu–O ] motif being identified as the primary active center for non-oxidative ethane dehydrogenation. This conclusion is robustly supported by quasi-in situ EPR (renumbered Supplementary Fig. 11) and in situ NAP-XPS (Figs. 5a and 5b) analyses, which consistently show that catalyst deactivation process is always accompanied by a pronounced decrease in the Cu2+ signal (associated with the [Cu–O ] motif). Under CO co-feeding conditions, the catalytic performance remains stable and the Cu2+ content is effectively maintained, further highlighting the central role of [Cu–O ] in sustaining activity.
To further clarify the role of [Cu–O ] and strengthen the assignment of [Cu–O ] as the main active site, we performed additional DFT calculations comparing β–H activation of the ·C H intermediate on these two motifs, guided by the active-species quenching experiments in Fig. 4b, which indicate that Cu sites are responsible for β–H activation. The results (please see renumbered Supplementary Fig. 32) reveal that on the most representative [Cu–O ] motif, the reaction energy for β–H bond cleavage in the ·C H intermediate is as high as 1.06 eV, indicating a strongly endergonic process. In sharp contrast, the same C–H activation step on the [Cu–O ] motif exhibits a much lower reaction energy of only 0.11 eV. This pronounced energy difference clearly demonstrates that [Cu–O ] ensembles as the key active centers for β–H activation, whereas [Cu–O ] ensembles make only a minor contribution to this crucial step.
Admittedly, due to the objective limitations of catalyst synthesis methods and the complexity of Cu valence state regulation, the existence of the [Cu–O ] structure is an intrinsic characteristic of the current system. Nevertheless, its presence does not affect the identification of the main active site. To further clarify the conclusion regarding [Cu–O ] as the primary active center, relevant insights have been comprehensively incorporated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 12, second paragraph), offering a more rigorous and coherent mechanistic explanation for the structure-activity relationship of the catalytic system.

Comment 3: In the tests, the authors found that CO production showed strong positive correlation with C H but remained insensitive to CO , suggesting CO yield is indirectly driven by C H conversion. How?
Response: We greatly appreciate your valuable comments, which help us clarify the mechanism more clearly and facilitate readers' understanding. Our interpretation is that under C H /CO co-feeding, CO originates primarily from the reduction of CO driven by a small amount of surface *H generated during the selective dehydrogenation of ethane, followed by CO formation. Because the formation of *H is governed by the activation and conversion rate of C H , the CO yield increases with C H conversion. Under our experimental conditions, the CO supply is sufficient and its involvement does not constitute the rate-limiting step, which explains the observed insensitivity of CO formation to changes in CO concentration.
This mechanism is supported by two lines of evidence. First, no CO was observed in the H /CO co-feeding control experiment (Fig. 4g), excluding the dominant redox-type RWGS pathway driven by molecular H activation under the present conditions. Second, in situ NAP-XPS and in situ infrared results show that ethane dehydrogenation can generate detectable surface *H signals, and *H is consumed under CO atmosphere (Figs. 5a and 5b). To present the above mechanism more intuitively, we have strengthened the corresponding discussion in the revised manuscript and supplemented a detailed analysis of the CO formation pathway (Please see the revised manuscript, page 10, second paragraph and page 12, first paragraph). In addition, following your Comment 4, we have incorporated DFT results on the involvement of CO , providing a more systematic elucidation of the CO formation pathway (Please see Comment 4). These revisions are intended to help readers accurately understand the reaction process.

Response: We sincerely appreciate your valuable comment. In response, we have now conducted additional DFT calculations to explicitly evaluate the involvement of CO in the photocatalytic process. These new results have been incorporated into the revised manuscript and Supplementary Information.
As outlined in the manuscript, the *H generated from β–H desorption at the O site does not readily desorb as H due to the high barrier of H–H coupling, leading to the deactivation of [Cu–O ] sites via *H coverage. Further calculations show that while direct reaction of *H with CO is thermodynamically unfavorable (∆G=3.5 eV), *H can combine with another *H at a neighboring O site to form H O with a low barrier of 0.40 eV, accompanied by the transformation of [Cu–O ] to [Cu–O ] (please see renumbered Supplementary Fig. 37). It should be noted that this dehydration step is still thermodynamically endergonic. This implies that, if the resulting [Cu–O ] structure cannot undergo further transformation, the *H species will thermodynamically tend to remain adsorbed, which is consistent with our experimental observation of *H buildup under a pure C H atmosphere. Under CO co‑feeding, CO cooperates with ·C H radicals from other sites to restore the [Cu–O ] structure via the *COOH pathway. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 37, adsorbed CO abstracts a β–H from ·C H to form *COOH (barrier: 1.32 eV), which then readily decomposes to adsorbed CO (barrier: 0.04 eV). After CO desorption, the [Cu–O ] site is regenerated and can continue to participate in β–H elimination, with the released *H subsequently coupling to form H . By contrast, direct CO dissociation via the MvK mechanism requires overcoming a much higher activation barrier (1.96 eV) and reaction energy (1.85 eV) (see Response Fig. R1), further corroborating the relative feasibility of the aforementioned cooperative pathway. These findings have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 13, first paragraph), and we appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments.

Comment 2: The activity evaluation relies mainly on a batch reactor, yet the Batch-type performance test section does not report the pressure. In a sealed batch reactor the pressure evolves during reaction and this can inflate apparent activity. Please report initial and final pressures, and how pressure changes over time. In addition, surface temperature measurement needs clarification. Please specify the measurement method, the emissivity used for infrared measurements, and the calibration procedure. Different emissivity values can lead to large differences in the measured temperature.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful comments, which have provided important guidance for improving our experimental design and data presentation. In accordance with your suggestions, we have revised the manuscript and supplemented the relevant descriptions as follows.
First, regarding your concern that the time evolution of pressure in the sealed batch reactor may influence the apparent activity, we have added in situ records of the pressure difference, defined as the difference between the instantaneous pressure and the initial pressure, as a function of time, as well as the catalyst surface temperature as a function of time, under a reaction atmosphere of 20 vol% C H /20 vol% CO /Ar (please see renumbered Supplementary Fig. 12). In these experiments, the initial pressure in the reactor was 1.0 atm, and a AS511A digital differential manometer (SMART SENSOR) was used to continuously monitor the pressure during the reaction. The results show that, immediately after the introduction of light irradiation, the system pressure increases rapidly, which can be mainly attributed to enhanced gas molecular motion induced by the photothermal effect. This was followed by a slow and nearly linear pressure increase, corresponding to the ongoing C H dehydrogenation reaction. It is important to emphasize that throughout the entire reaction process, the maximum pressure increase is less than 10 kPa, which is below 10% of the initial pressure. Therefore, we consider that the pressure variation within this range has a negligible influence on the reaction rate and the evaluation of apparent activity and does not compromise the reliability of the conclusions. The descriptions of relevant data and corresponding measurement methods have been clearly integrated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 7, second paragraph and page 14, “Batch-type performance test” section).
Second, regarding the measurement of the catalyst surface temperature and the procedure for setting and calibrating the emissivity (ε), we have provided a detailed description in the “Methods” section of the revised manuscript. Specifically, the catalyst surface temperature was mainly monitored using a Uti160S infrared thermal imager (UNI-T). During the experiments, the camera was fixed at an oblique angle above the reactor and focused on the top surface of the catalyst bed in order to acquire thermal images of the catalyst layer. The emissivity of the camera was set to ε = 0.95. This value was obtained through an empirical calibration procedure in which a thin, uniformly spread layer of catalyst powder was placed at the center of a pre-calibrated heating plate. The temperature of the heating plate was successively set to 50, 100, 150, and 200°C, and the emissivity parameter of the thermal imager was adjusted until the infrared readings of the catalyst surface at each temperature matched the actual temperature of the heating plate as closely as possible. The resulting emissivity value was then used in all subsequent temperature measurements. In addition, to further verify the accuracy of the temperature measurements, we simultaneously recorded the catalyst surface temperature as a function of time using a K-type thermocouple under identical reaction conditions, as shown in renumbered Supplementary Fig. 12. The temperatures obtained from the thermocouple show excellent agreement with those measured by the infrared thermal camera, which provides additional confirmation of the reliability of the temperature measurement method. The complete calibration procedure of the thermal imager and the detailed protocol for surface temperature measurement have been systematically added to the “Methods” section of the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 14, “Batch-type performance test” section).
We again sincerely thank you for your careful review and valuable comments, which have significantly improved the completeness and transparency of the manuscript with respect to the description of experimental methods and the rigor of the data.

Comment 9: Cu/TiO is widely reported for RWGS. Why was no CO detected in the H /CO control experiment?
Response: We sincerely thank you for raising this important question. Indeed, Cu-based catalysts are widely recognized as promising candidates for the RWGS reaction owing to their weak CO adsorption and facile CO desorption. However, the RWGS reaction is highly temperature-sensitive, which is the key reason why no CO was detected in our H /CO co-feeding control experiment carried out at a low temperature (108°C).
Inherently, the RWGS reaction is an endergonic reaction (ΔH° ≈ +41.2 kJ·mol-1). In traditional thermal catalysis systems, Cu-based catalysts typically require temperatures of ≥300°C to be significantly activated to initiate the reaction and generate CO at detectable levels (DOI: 10.1016/j.cej.2025.165414, 10.1021/jacs.3c01336, 10.1021/acscatal.0c01584). Although photothermal synergy strategies developed in recent years have effectively reduced the reaction's onset temperature threshold, existing studies indicate that even the current state-of-the-art Cu-based RWGS catalytic systems still maintain an onset temperature of no less than 150°C. For instance, the high-entropy alloy Cu catalyst developed by Xiong's group (DOI: 10.1002/adma.202409689) and the high-entropy oxide Cu-based catalyst (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-38889-5) reported by Ye's group both require temperatures above 220°C for CO generation to be detected; while the Cu single-atom doped In O photothermal catalyst subsequently developed by Xiong's group further reduced the reaction temperature, its RWGS activity onset threshold remains at 150°C (DOI: 10.1002/anie.202505244).
Based on the above analysis, the absence of CO in the H /CO co-feed control is consistent with prior reports and is more likely attributable to differences in reaction conditions, particularly the low temperature used in our work, which is insufficient to trigger the RWGS reaction. Furthermore, given that CO is detectable under C H /CO co-feeding, we infer that, under the present reaction conditions, this catalyst likely lacks sufficiently active sites for H activation and is therefore unable to efficiently initiate a redox-type RWGS pathway. This interpretation has been explicitly incorporated into the revised manuscript for clarification (Please see the revised manuscript, page 10, second paragraph).

Response：We greatly appreciate your insightful comments and reminder, which are invaluable for strengthening the rigor of our mechanism analysis. We fully acknowledge the concern that quenchers may alter the surface properties of the catalyst or the adsorption behavior of reactant molecules, thereby introducing uncertainty into the mechanistic interpretation. This limitation is in fact common to conventional quenching experiments, which are usually based on the idealized assumption that sacrificial agents selectively remove the targeted reactive species without inducing other interfering effects. To assess the reliability of the mechanistic conclusions drawn from the quenching experiments in this work, we supplemented with additional control and cross-check experiments that were specifically aimed at minimizing potential interference arising from non-specific effects.
First, additional photoluminescence measurements were carried out to verify the effective quenching of photogenerated charges by the employed scavengers (please see renumbered Supplementary Fig. 16). Upon introduction of either hole or electron scavengers into the Cu /TiO system, the fluorescence intensity decreased markedly, confirming that the selected scavengers efficiently capture the targeted charge carriers. Second, in order to exclude possible interference of the quenchers with C H adsorption or the local surface environment, we performed cross validation experiments using alternative scavengers with distinct structures and chemical properties, that is, sodium oxalate (Na C O ) as a hole scavenger and potassium dichromate (K Cr O ) as an electron scavenger. As shown in the optimized Fig. 4b (Please see the revised manuscript, page 8, Fig. 4b), the product formation rates and distribution profiles obtained with these alternative scavengers are highly consistent with those observed in the original system. These results indicate that the observed quenching effects mainly arise from the selective removal of the targeted reactive species, rather than from indirect perturbations of the surface properties induced by the quencher.
Furthermore, in the analysis of the results, we considered not only changes in overall catalytic activity but also the evolution of product distribution. For instance, in the electron quenching experiments, the H /C H ratio decreased significantly, indicating that photogenerated electrons play a key role in the kinetics of H formation. Such selective changes in product distribution are difficult to attribute solely to modifications in C H adsorption behavior. In addition, the experiments targeting Cu sites were designed by using NH to selectively coordinate with Cu and thereby deliberately switch off its catalytic function. This strategy is inherently intended to probe the role of a specific type of active site and does not rely on the assumption that all other processes remain completely unaffected. As a result, the corresponding data more directly reflect the functional role of Cu sites in the reaction.
Based on the above supplementary data and analyses, we have revised and refined the mechanistic discussion in the manuscript in order to clarify how non-specific effects of the quenchers and NH on surface properties and adsorption behavior were minimized or excluded (Please see the revised manuscript, page 8,9).

Comment 17: The way the ethyl is coordinated to the surface as shown in the *C H +*H panel in Fig. 5c seems odd for an intermediate (unless it’s a transition state), since based on coordination chemistry principles one would expect coordination through the carbon – is there experimental evidence supporting H-coordination to the surface?

Indeed, direct experimental identification of such a configuration is challenging due to the transient nature of surface intermediates. However, according to the theory of agostic interaction, the computed structure is chemically reasonable. In this configuration, the surface metal atom interacts with the σ (C–H) bond of the ethyl group, forming a three-center two-electron (3c–2e) M···H–C bond. Such agostic-like interactions are known to enable electron donation from the C–H σ bond to an empty orbital of the metal center, thereby stabilizing alkyl intermediates and facilitating β-C–H activation or elimination. This type of H-coordination has been widely observed in both homogeneous organometallic complexes and heterogeneous metal or oxide surfaces. This process generates a free •C H radical and an adsorbed *H at the O site. The •C H radical then undergoes two successive mild endergonic steps to transfer a *H to the Cu site via the HAT mechanism, involving adsorption at Cu site (0.29 eV) followed by β–H cleavage with a reaction energy of only 0.11 eV. In contrast, although the C–H activation ability of O site is also significantly enhanced after trapping photogenerated holes, with the corresponding barriers being comparable to that at O site, the resulting •C H radical exhibits an adsorption energy of 0.58 eV at the five-coordinated Ti site (Ti ), and the subsequent β–H bond cleavage has a reaction energy as high as 1.60 eV (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 31), both of which are significantly larger than those on the Cu site. This demonstrates that the introduction of Cu not only markedly promotes the efficient localization of photogenerated holes from the bulk to surface O sites, but also facilitates the •C H adsorption and β–H activation capabilities. This synergistic advantage in both hole management and β–H activation underpins the high ethane activation capability and excellent ethylene selectivity of the Cu /TiO catalyst. In addition, the high reaction energy for β–H cleavage at the Cu+ site in [Cu–O ] (1.06 eV) further confirms its limited activity, highlighting [Cu–O ] as the dominant active center (Supplementary Fig. 32). Finally, we calculated the generation of H at the [Cu–O] units, where *H–*H coupling energy barrier is 0.79 eV. Notably, •C H is also possible to continue to activate the β–H bond via hole-trapped O with an energy barrier of 0.07 eV (Supplementary Fig. 33), following the first C–H bond cleavage mechanism. The resulting *H is captured by the O adjacent to [Cu–O] units. Consequently, the H formation is significantly hindered at the O and O sites (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 34), with an energy barrier as high as 2.79 eV.

Response: We sincerely thank you for this valuable comment. In this work, on-site Hubbard U corrections were applied to both Ti 3d and O 2p orbitals to more properly describe the localized electronic states associated with photoexcited charge carriers. The U value of 4.2 eV for Ti 3d orbitals was adopted based on previous computational studies of TiO , which demonstrated that this value accurately reproduces the experimental band gap and electronic structure of TiO (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.82.144119; 10.1016/j.susc.2007.08.025; 10.1039/c1cp21547g). In addition, a U correction was applied to the O 2p orbitals to cancel the self-interaction error and facilitate the localization of photogenerated holes on surface O sites. This approach has been successfully employed in several earlier DFT+U studies to model hole trapping and defect-related electronic states in TiO and related oxides. (DOI: 10.1038/s41929-018-0055-z; 10.1021/acscatal.2c01339). We have now added an explicit explanation of this choice in the “Theoretical calculations” section of the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 16-17, “Theoretical calculations” section).

In particular this means that the molecules are free to rotate and translate subject to the above constraint, and in addition the TiO surface are allowed to relax. Response to Reviewer #4
General Comment: This manuscript by Lingzhi Wang and coworkers reported a site-defined photocatalytic strategy for the selective light-driven dehydrogenation of ethane (C H ) to ethylene (C H ) using atomically dispersed Cu–O ensembles on TiO (Cu /TiO ). The study highlights that Cu atoms coordinated with bridging oxygen form well-defined [Cu–O] motifs, which serve as active centers for stepwise C–H activation and H evolution. Photogenerated holes localize at O sites to initiate the first C–H cleavage, while adjacent Cu centers mediate β–H elimination, resulting in efficient and hydrogen-conserving C H upgrading. This catalyst achieved an impressive C H yield of 21.1 mmol g-1 h-1, 97% C H selectivity, and a quantum efficiency of 6.1% at 365 nm, outperforming state-of-the-art photocatalytic ethane dehydrogenation systems. The co-feeding of CO was found to selectively scavenge surface *H species, thereby preventing catalyst deactivation and preserving long-term activity. The mechanism is well-supported by a combination of in situ EPR, DRIFTS, NAP-XPS, TRFL, fs-TAS, and DFT calculations, which collectively reveal that [Cu–O] ensembles orchestrate cooperative charge transfer and redox functionality, enabling controlled C–H activation and H evolution under mild conditions. This paper provides atomic-level insight into the design of redox-cooperative single-atom photocatalysts for alkane upgrading and contributes significantly to the development of sustainable, low-temperature C–H activation chemistry. This paper will be potentially acceptable for publication in Nature Communications. However, I do not recommend publication in the present form because some questions need to be answered.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your recognition of our study’s potential and your valuable insights. Your comments have provided crucial guidance for us to clarify key points and deepen our analysis, thereby significantly enhancing the overall quality of our work. All the concerns you raised have been point-by-point and thoroughly addressed in the revised manuscript. We believe that the revised version now fully meets the publication standards of Nature Communications, with point-by-point responses presented below.
Comment 1. The authors' characterization (XPS, XAS) clearly indicates that the as-prepared catalyst contains a substantial fraction of Cu+ (approx. 38% based on XPS deconvolution), coexisting with Cu2+. The manuscript's mechanistic discussion, however, focuses almost exclusively on the role of the [Cu2+−O ] motif as the primary active site for C-H activation and H evolution. The role of the significant initial population of [Cu+−O ] sites remains ambiguous. Are the Cu+ sites catalytically active for any step of the reaction, or are they merely spectators? Can these sites act as electron traps or play another role in the charge carrier dynamics that influence the overall efficiency? Is there any evidence for the interconversion between Cu+ and Cu2+ under reaction conditions, beyond the deactivation pathway identified?
Response: We sincerely appreciate your in-depth attention to the potential role of Cu+ species ([Cu+−O ] motif). Given that Comment 1 and Comment 10 are closely related, we present a consolidated response herein to more clearly address your questions regarding the roles of different Cu species in the reaction. By combining in situ spectroscopic characterization with first principles calculations, we can identify the [Cu–O ] unit as the primary active center, whereas the [Cu–O ] motif is essentially inactive. Quasi-in situ EPR (renumbered Supplementary Fig. 11) and in situ NAP-XPS (Figs. 5a and 5b) results consistently show that under feed conditions containing only C H the catalyst deactivation is accompanied by a pronounced decrease in the Cu2+ signal associated with [Cu–O ], whereas under co-feeding of C H and CO the catalytic activity remains stable and the Cu2+ content is effectively preserved, which provides strong experimental support for the core role of [Cu–O ] in the reaction.
With respect to the question of “Is there any evidence for the interconversion between Cu+ and Cu2+ under reaction conditions, beyond the deactivation pathway identified?”, quasi-in situ Raman spectroscopy under stepwise feeding of C H and CO provides relevant support. Under a C H atmosphere, the Eg vibrational mode of TiO gradually shifts to higher wavenumbers with increasing reaction time (renumbered Supplementary Fig. 23), which can be attributed to unit-cell expansion or enhanced lattice strain in TiO induced by the reduction of Cu2+ to Cu+. When the gas atmosphere is switched from C H to CO , this blue shift is reversed. This reversible behavior indicates that a certain degree of dynamic adjustment between Cu+ and Cu2+ occurs during the reaction and that this redox equilibrium is strongly influenced by the presence of co-fed CO .
To strengthen the above conclusion and following your helpful suggestion in the comment 10, we have incorporated additional DFT calculations in the revised manuscript for the β–H bond activation of the ·C H radical at both types of Cu sites (please see renumbered Supplementary Fig. 32). We focus on the β–H activation step because radical scavenger experiments (Fig. 4b) indicate that, in this system, Cu mainly participates in β–H bond activation processes. The calculations show that at a representative [Cu–O ] site, the reaction energy for cleavage of the β–H bond in the ·C H intermediate is as high as 1.06 eV, indicating a clearly endergonic process, whereas at the [Cu–O ] site the barrier for the same step is only 0.11 eV. This pronounced difference in activation energy clearly demonstrates that [Cu–O ] is the key active center for β–H bond activation, while the direct contribution of [Cu–O ] to this critical step is rather limited. All computational results have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 12, second paragraph).
Meanwhile, we fully understand your concern regarding whether Cu+ might play a beneficial role in charge separation and transport. However, due to limitations in current synthesis strategies and the lack of precise control over copper valence states, the presence of the [Cu–O ] motif is an inherent feature of the current catalytic system that is difficult to completely eliminate, and it is experimentally challenging to adjust the Cu2+/Cu+ ratio in an accurate and independent manner. As a result, we are not yet able to isolate and quantitatively evaluate the specific contribution of Cu+ as an electron trap or as a charge modulation center. This is indeed a limitation of the present study, which we have explicitly acknowledged in the revised manuscript, and we regard it as an important direction for future efforts to further optimize and extend this catalytic system. It should be emphasized that even if Cu+ were to contribute to improved charge separation or transport to some extent, its influence remains non-decisive, and it does not challenge the core conclusion that Cu2+ serves as the dominant center for β–H bond activation. All experimental and theoretical results consistently support this judgment. In the revised manuscript, we have further strengthened the mechanistic discussion to enhance its rigor and coherence.

Comment 2. The authors report a catalyst surface temperature of ~108 °C under illumination. While the control experiments (wavelength dependence, dark controls, and a significantly lower activation energy under light) provide strong evidence for a predominantly photocatalytic mechanism, the potential contribution of a photothermal effect at this temperature warrants a more detailed discussion. Response: Thank you for your insightful comments and valuable suggestions, which have further improved the quality of our manuscript. We fully understand the core concern regarding decoupling and quantifying the contributions of quantum effects and light-induced thermal effects, a key and challenging issue in the field of photocatalysis that urgently requires clarification.
Given that phonon vibrations, or thermal energy, are inherent properties of materials under illumination, photothermal effects are indeed unavoidable in photocatalytic processes. Their mechanisms of action are notably complex. On one hand, thermal effects can influence catalytic performance through pathways unrelated to quantum efficiency, such as promoting reactant diffusion and optimizing molecular adsorption on catalyst surfaces. On the other hand, increased temperature may also act through processes related to quantum efficiency, including enhancing charge carrier migration and separation efficiency or accelerating carrier recombination (DOI: 10.1016/j.cej.2022.137063, 10.1021/acscatal.4c03685). Therefore, completely decoupling and quantitatively distinguishing their respective contributions at the microscopic scale remains a significant challenge in the field. Admittedly, progress has been made in quantifying thermal and non-thermal effects in plasmonic catalysis. For instance, He's group designed precise control experiments to selectively "switch off" pathways such as charge transfer, thereby isolating the contribution of individual mechanisms (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-57569-0). Zhang's group measured the actual reaction temperature in photothermal catalysis based on Le Chatelier's principle and calculated the "pure hot electron contribution" by subtracting the thermal effect rate from the total reaction rate under illumination (DOI: 10.1002/anie.202304452). Nevertheless, most of these studies have not systematically considered the temperature-dependent influence of photothermal effects on charge carrier dynamics, which may, to some extent, underestimate the complex role of photothermal effects.
Given the current state of research, there is no universal approach to quantify the contribution of light-induced thermal effects. Therefore, we have attempted to qualitatively evaluate the influence of the photothermal effect at the macroscopic level. Specifically, we additionally designed a control experiment in which an external ice bath was introduced to suppress the temperature rise of the system under the condition of maintaining the same light intensity, thereby distinguishing the photothermal contribution. The results of this experiment have been included in the revised manuscript as renumbered Supplementary Fig. 10. The data show that when an ice bath was used to weaken the photothermal effect, the catalytic performance decreased significantly from 8.4 mmol g-1 h-1 to 3.8 mmol g-1 h-1， while the product selectivity remained unaffected. Therefore, based on this new data and our existing evidence (wavelength dependence, dark controls, significantly reduced activation energy), we conclude that the process is best described as a photon-driven, phonon-assisted mechanism. In this mechanism, photogenerated charge carriers serve as the primary driving force and dictate the reaction pathway, while light-induced thermal effects (phonon assistance) play an auxiliary role by potentially optimizing processes such as diffusion and adsorption or moderately regulating carrier behavior.
We have added the above analysis in the revised manuscript to further clarify the relationship between these two effects (Please see the revised manuscript, page 7, first paragraph). Once again, we appreciate your suggestions, which have helped us refine the mechanistic arguments.

In response to your comments, we have provided the following clarifications based on our experimental data.
First, it should be noted that the CO yield detected in both continuous-flow and batch reactor tests remained below 0.1 mmol g-1 h-1, which is considered a trace amount. Throughout the 20-hour stability test, no significant decline in catalytic activity was observed. Furthermore, in situ DRIFTS under C H and CO co-feeding conditions did not detect any carbonyl species on the catalyst surface. These results collectively suggest a low risk of CO-induced poisoning of the Cu active sites under the current reaction conditions.
Regarding the possibility of the RWGS side reaction, control experiments involving H and CO co-feeding, as shown in Fig. 4g, clearly demonstrate that this reaction does not occur in our system. The core reason for this phenomenon is that the Cu /TiO catalyst lacks active sites for H activation and the reaction system operates at a low temperature, which prevents the initiation of the RWGS reaction through the redox mechanism. As for the detected trace CO, its specific formation mechanism involves the following process. During C H dehydrogenation, ethane undergoes a continuous dehydrogenation side reaction on lattice oxygen. This process increases the energy barrier for H formation, leading to partial *H species failing to desorb in a timely manner, then induces the subsequent conversion of CO to CO.
To more clearly illustrate the formation pathway of CO and address concerns about the RWGS side reaction, we have supplemented detailed discussions and explanations of the CO formation mechanism in the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 10, second paragraph and page 12, first paragraph).

To clarify the site-dependent reactivity and selectivity, we have additionally computed C–H activation and β–H activation capabilities at different sites. We note that on the anatase TiO (101) surface, all exposed Ti atoms are fivefold-coordinated (Ti ) and adjacent to bridging oxygens (O ). Therefore, the O configuration essentially represents the terrace Ti site on this surface. The C–H activation structure at the O site is thus equivalent to that at the terrace Ti site, and both correspond to the same local coordination environment of Ti . In contrast, although the C–H activation ability of O site is also significantly enhanced after trapping photogenerated holes, with the corresponding barriers being comparable to that at O site, the resulting •C H radical exhibits an adsorption energy of 0.58 eV at the five-coordinated Ti site (Ti ), and the subsequent β–H bond cleavage has a reaction energy as high as 1.60 eV (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 31), both of which are significantly larger than those on the Cu site. This demonstrates that the introduction of Cu not only markedly promotes the efficient localization of photogenerated holes from the bulk to surface O sites, but also facilitates the •C H adsorption and β–H activation capabilities. This synergistic advantage in both hole management and β–H activation underpins the high ethane activation capability and excellent ethylene selectivity of the Cu /TiO catalyst. In addition, the high reaction energy for β–H cleavage at the Cu+ site in [Cu–O ] (1.06 eV) further confirms its limited activity, highlighting [Cu–O ] as the dominant active center (Supplementary Fig. 32).
Comment 8. The calculated barriers for *H migration (2.9–3.1 eV) are high, supporting the conclusion of *H accumulation. However, the authors could further discuss whether such high-energy events are still feasible under photon-driven conditions (where local hot carriers may contribute). The neglect of non-adiabatic effects may lead to an underestimation of possible *H dynamics.
Response: We greatly appreciate your insightful comment regarding the potential role of non-adiabatic effects and hot-carrier–driven dynamics in facilitating *H migration. Indeed, under photon-driven conditions, energetic carriers may transiently modify reaction pathways. We fully acknowledge this possibility. However, previous studies show that hot-carrier relax extremely rapidly through electron–electron and electron–phonon scattering, so that only a very small fraction (<2%) can cross the interface before thermalization. (DOI: 10.1038/s41377-021-00609-3) Because hot-electron injection competes directly with ultrafast self-scattering, the available energy cannot be efficiently delivered to drive processes requiring high barriers. In addition, given that the vast majority of hot carriers lose their excess energy within tens to hundreds of femtoseconds (DOI: 10.1021/nn305080c; https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.57.12812; https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.67.113315). The efficiency of hot-carriers–assisted *H migration is likely very low, and our conclusion regarding *H accumulation remains robust.
Comment 9. The proposed *H scavenging pathway via CO → *COOH → CO is strongly supported by DRIFTS and isotope labeling, but the DFT section only briefly covers CO reactivity. It would strengthen the work if the energy profile for *COOH formation and decomposition were presented explicitly, in parallel with the C H dehydrogenation pathway.
Response: We greatly appreciate your valuable suggestions and insightful comments. Following your recommendation, calculations for the CO →*COOH→CO pathway have been added, which are presented in the Supplementary Information due to length considerations. As outlined in manuscript, when the β–H species of C H desorbs at the O site, the resulting *H cannot readily desorb as H because H–H coupling is associated with a high activation barrier, leading to deactivation of the [Cu–O ] active centers due to *H surface accumulation. Further DFT calculations reveal that while the direct reaction between this *H species and CO to form CO and H O is thermodynamically hindered due to its high reaction energy (△G=3.5 eV), the *H can instead combine with another *H at a neighboring O site to form and desorb as H O, with a modest barrier of only 0.40 eV and is accompanied by a structural transformation from [Cu–O ] to [Cu–O ]. Under CO co-feeding conditions, CO cooperates with ·C H generated at other active sites, enabling the structural regeneration of the catalyst from [Cu-O ] to [Cu-O ] via the *COOH pathway. As shown in renumbered Supplementary Fig. 37, CO first adsorbs at the [Cu–O ] site, and the adsorbed CO then abstracts a β–H from ·C H to form an adsorbed *COOH intermediate, with an activation barrier of 1.32 eV and a reaction energy of 0.29 eV. In contrast, direct oxygen-vacancy refilling by CO via a Mars–van Krevelen (MvK) mechanism is less favorable both thermodynamically and kinetically, with an activation barrier and reaction energy as high as 1.96 eV and 1.85 eV, respectively (Fig. R3). The resulting *COOH subsequently decomposes into adsorbed CO with a barrier of only 0.04 eV. After CO desorption, the [Cu–O ] coordination environment is regenerated. Following the reaction pathway illustrated in renumbered Supplementary Fig. 37, the regenerated Cu sites can further capture β–H, which then couples with *H species at O sites to produce H . It is worth emphasizing that *H removal via H O formation remains an endergonic process, implying that under pure C H the system tends to retain *H on the catalyst surface rather than efficiently removing it through the H O pathway. The introduction of CO promotes the continuous conversion of [Cu–O ] back to [Cu–O ], thereby facilitating *H conversion toward H O from kinetic perspectives. This provides a rational explanation for the absence of observable *H accumulation on the catalyst surface under CO co-feeding. These results have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 13, first paragraph), and we once again thank the reviewer for the thorough and constructive suggestions.
