Comment 19: For the computational methods, a +U correction is typically not applied to the oxygen but only the metal – if there’s any special reason for this it should be discussed; for the Ti, why was 4.2 eV chosen (is there a reference to it an experimental/computational benchmark?)
Response: We sincerely thank you for this valuable comment. In this work, on-site Hubbard U corrections were applied to both Ti 3d and O 2p orbitals to more properly describe the localized electronic states associated with photoexcited charge carriers. The U value of 4.2 eV for Ti 3d orbitals was adopted based on previous computational studies of TiO , which demonstrated that this value accurately reproduces the experimental band gap and electronic structure of TiO (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.82.144119; 10.1016/j.susc.2007.08.025; 10.1039/c1cp21547g). In addition, a U correction was applied to the O 2p orbitals to cancel the self-interaction error and facilitate the localization of photogenerated holes on surface O sites. This approach has been successfully employed in several earlier DFT+U studies to model hole trapping and defect-related electronic states in TiO and related oxides. (DOI: 10.1038/s41929-018-0055-z; 10.1021/acscatal.2c01339). We have now added an explicit explanation of this choice in the “Theoretical calculations” section of the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 16-17, “Theoretical calculations” section).

Comment 21: For the TS search, how the constrained optimization technique was used should be discussed.
Response: We sincerely thank you for this insightful comment. The transition states (TSs) were searched by a constrained optimization scheme. In this approach, we keep the C-H bond distance fixed at preselected values, and minimize the total energy with respect to all remaining orthogonal degrees of freedom. In particular this means that the molecules are free to rotate and translate subject to the above constraint, and in addition the TiO surface are allowed to relax. The TSs were verified when (i) all forces on the atoms vanish and (ii) the total energy is a maximum along the reaction coordinate but a minimum with respect to the rest of the degrees of freedom. Previous work has demonstrated that the above DFT setup affords a good accuracy, especially for the calculation of reaction barriers in heterogeneous catalysis (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.80.3650; 10.1021/ja0207551). These methodological details on the TS search have now been explicitly added to the “Theoretical calculations” section of the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 17, “Theoretical calculations” section).

Response to Reviewer #4
General Comment: This manuscript by Lingzhi Wang and coworkers reported a site-defined photocatalytic strategy for the selective light-driven dehydrogenation of ethane (C H ) to ethylene (C H ) using atomically dispersed Cu–O ensembles on TiO (Cu /TiO ). The study highlights that Cu atoms coordinated with bridging oxygen form well-defined [Cu–O] motifs, which serve as active centers for stepwise C–H activation and H evolution. Photogenerated holes localize at O sites to initiate the first C–H cleavage, while adjacent Cu centers mediate β–H elimination, resulting in efficient and hydrogen-conserving C H upgrading. This catalyst achieved an impressive C H yield of 21.1 mmol g-1 h-1, 97% C H selectivity, and a quantum efficiency of 6.1% at 365 nm, outperforming state-of-the-art photocatalytic ethane dehydrogenation systems. The co-feeding of CO was found to selectively scavenge surface *H species, thereby preventing catalyst deactivation and preserving long-term activity. The mechanism is well-supported by a combination of in situ EPR, DRIFTS, NAP-XPS, TRFL, fs-TAS, and DFT calculations, which collectively reveal that [Cu–O] ensembles orchestrate cooperative charge transfer and redox functionality, enabling controlled C–H activation and H evolution under mild conditions. This paper provides atomic-level insight into the design of redox-cooperative single-atom photocatalysts for alkane upgrading and contributes significantly to the development of sustainable, low-temperature C–H activation chemistry. This paper will be potentially acceptable for publication in Nature Communications. However, I do not recommend publication in the present form because some questions need to be answered.

Comment 1. The authors' characterization (XPS, XAS) clearly indicates that the as-prepared catalyst contains a substantial fraction of Cu+ (approx. 38% based on XPS deconvolution), coexisting with Cu2+. The manuscript's mechanistic discussion, however, focuses almost exclusively on the role of the [Cu2+−O ] motif as the primary active site for C-H activation and H evolution. The role of the significant initial population of [Cu+−O ] sites remains ambiguous. Are the Cu+ sites catalytically active for any step of the reaction, or are they merely spectators? Response: We sincerely appreciate your in-depth attention to the potential role of Cu+ species ([Cu+−O ] motif). Given that Comment 1 and Comment 10 are closely related, we present a consolidated response herein to more clearly address your questions regarding the roles of different Cu species in the reaction. By combining in situ spectroscopic characterization with first principles calculations, we can identify the [Cu–O ] unit as the primary active center, whereas the [Cu–O ] motif is essentially inactive. Quasi-in situ EPR (renumbered Supplementary Fig. 11) and in situ NAP-XPS (Figs. 5a and 5b) results consistently show that under feed conditions containing only C H the catalyst deactivation is accompanied by a pronounced decrease in the Cu2+ signal associated with [Cu–O ], whereas under co-feeding of C H and CO the catalytic activity remains stable and the Cu2+ content is effectively preserved, which provides strong experimental support for the core role of [Cu–O ] in the reaction.
With respect to the question of “Is there any evidence for the interconversion between Cu+ and Cu2+ under reaction conditions, beyond the deactivation pathway identified?”, quasi-in situ Raman spectroscopy under stepwise feeding of C H and CO provides relevant support. Under a C H atmosphere, the Eg vibrational mode of TiO gradually shifts to higher wavenumbers with increasing reaction time (renumbered Supplementary Fig. 23), which can be attributed to unit-cell expansion or enhanced lattice strain in TiO induced by the reduction of Cu2+ to Cu+. When the gas atmosphere is switched from C H to CO , this blue shift is reversed. This reversible behavior indicates that a certain degree of dynamic adjustment between Cu+ and Cu2+ occurs during the reaction and that this redox equilibrium is strongly influenced by the presence of co-fed CO .
To strengthen the above conclusion and following your helpful suggestion in the comment 10, we have incorporated additional DFT calculations in the revised manuscript for the β–H bond activation of the ·C H radical at both types of Cu sites (please see renumbered Supplementary Fig. 32). We focus on the β–H activation step because radical scavenger experiments (Fig. 4b) indicate that, in this system, Cu mainly participates in β–H bond activation processes. The calculations show that at a representative [Cu–O ] site, the reaction energy for cleavage of the β–H bond in the ·C H intermediate is as high as 1.06 eV, indicating a clearly endergonic process, whereas at the [Cu–O ] site the barrier for the same step is only 0.11 eV. This pronounced difference in activation energy clearly demonstrates that [Cu–O ] is the key active center for β–H bond activation, while the direct contribution of [Cu–O ] to this critical step is rather limited. All computational results have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 12, second paragraph).
Meanwhile, we fully understand your concern regarding whether Cu+ might play a beneficial role in charge separation and transport. However, due to limitations in current synthesis strategies and the lack of precise control over copper valence states, the presence of the [Cu–O ] motif is an inherent feature of the current catalytic system that is difficult to completely eliminate, and it is experimentally challenging to adjust the Cu2+/Cu+ ratio in an accurate and independent manner. As a result, we are not yet able to isolate and quantitatively evaluate the specific contribution of Cu+ as an electron trap or as a charge modulation center. This is indeed a limitation of the present study, which we have explicitly acknowledged in the revised manuscript, and we regard it as an important direction for future efforts to further optimize and extend this catalytic system. It should be emphasized that even if Cu+ were to contribute to improved charge separation or transport to some extent, its influence remains non-decisive, and it does not challenge the core conclusion that Cu2+ serves as the dominant center for β–H bond activation. All experimental and theoretical results consistently support this judgment. In the revised manuscript, we have further strengthened the mechanistic discussion to enhance its rigor and coherence.

Comment 2. The authors report a catalyst surface temperature of ~108 °C under illumination. While the control experiments (wavelength dependence, dark controls, and a significantly lower activation energy under light) provide strong evidence for a predominantly photocatalytic mechanism, the potential contribution of a photothermal effect at this temperature warrants a more detailed discussion. A localized thermal effect could still play a role in overcoming certain reaction barriers. The authors should provide a more quantitative analysis or discussion to deconvolve the quantum effects from the light-induced thermal effects to strengthen their mechanistic claims further.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comments and valuable suggestions, which have further improved the quality of our manuscript. We fully understand the core concern regarding decoupling and quantifying the contributions of quantum effects and light-induced thermal effects, a key and challenging issue in the field of photocatalysis that urgently requires clarification.
Given that phonon vibrations, or thermal energy, are inherent properties of materials under illumination, photothermal effects are indeed unavoidable in photocatalytic processes. Their mechanisms of action are notably complex. On one hand, thermal effects can influence catalytic performance through pathways unrelated to quantum efficiency, such as promoting reactant diffusion and optimizing molecular adsorption on catalyst surfaces. On the other hand, increased temperature may also act through processes related to quantum efficiency, including enhancing charge carrier migration and separation efficiency or accelerating carrier recombination (DOI: 10.1016/j.cej.2022.137063, 10.1021/acscatal.4c03685). Therefore, completely decoupling and quantitatively distinguishing their respective contributions at the microscopic scale remains a significant challenge in the field. Admittedly, progress has been made in quantifying thermal and non-thermal effects in plasmonic catalysis. For instance, He's group designed precise control experiments to selectively "switch off" pathways such as charge transfer, thereby isolating the contribution of individual mechanisms (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-57569-0). Zhang's group measured the actual reaction temperature in photothermal catalysis based on Le Chatelier's principle and calculated the "pure hot electron contribution" by subtracting the thermal effect rate from the total reaction rate under illumination (DOI: 10.1002/anie.202304452). Nevertheless, most of these studies have not systematically considered the temperature-dependent influence of photothermal effects on charge carrier dynamics, which may, to some extent, underestimate the complex role of photothermal effects.
Given the current state of research, there is no universal approach to quantify the contribution of light-induced thermal effects. Therefore, we have attempted to qualitatively evaluate the influence of the photothermal effect at the macroscopic level. Specifically, we additionally designed a control experiment in which an external ice bath was introduced to suppress the temperature rise of the system under the condition of maintaining the same light intensity, thereby distinguishing the photothermal contribution. The results of this experiment have been included in the revised manuscript as renumbered Supplementary Fig. 10. The data show that when an ice bath was used to weaken the photothermal effect, the catalytic performance decreased significantly from 8.4 mmol g-1 h-1 to 3.8 mmol g-1 h-1， while the product selectivity remained unaffected. Therefore, based on this new data and our existing evidence (wavelength dependence, dark controls, significantly reduced activation energy), we conclude that the process is best described as a photon-driven, phonon-assisted mechanism. In this mechanism, photogenerated charge carriers serve as the primary driving force and dictate the reaction pathway, while light-induced thermal effects (phonon assistance) play an auxiliary role by potentially optimizing processes such as diffusion and adsorption or moderately regulating carrier behavior.
We have added the above analysis in the revised manuscript to further clarify the relationship between these two effects (Please see the revised manuscript, page 7, first paragraph). Once again, we appreciate your suggestions, which have helped us refine the mechanistic arguments.

Response: We sincerely thank you for your valuable suggestions and kind reminders. In this work, the excited-state surface was modeled by introducing a localized hole to mimic the photoexcited condition, following previous DFT-based studies on photocatalytic TiO systems. To simulate a photogenerated hole in the consideration of simplifying the complicated photo-excited system to exclude the uncertain electron–hole interaction which varies with the trapping center while ensuring the electroneutrality of the periodic system (eliminating the energy correction resulting from the presence of background counter charge), we introduced an OH group as an electron acceptor on the bottom surface of the slab instead of removing electrons from the periodic system. The lattice oxygen that captures a photogenerated hole exhibits distinct characteristics compared to that in the ground state, which can be readily identified by the following features: (1) The ground-state lattice oxygen has no distinct spin-polarizing features and excited-state lattice oxygen exhibits distinct spin behavior. (2) Geometry structures: the hole localization is accompanied by the distinct elongations of Ti–O bonds by the outward movement of the lattice Ti4+ ions. To clarify the site-dependent reactivity and selectivity, we have additionally computed C–H activation and β–H activation capabilities at different sites. We note that on the anatase TiO (101) surface, all exposed Ti atoms are fivefold-coordinated (Ti ) and adjacent to bridging oxygens (O ). Therefore, the O configuration essentially represents the terrace Ti site on this surface. The C–H activation structure at the O site is thus equivalent to that at the terrace Ti site, and both correspond to the same local coordination environment of Ti . The efficiency of hot-carriers–assisted *H migration is likely very low, and our conclusion regarding *H accumulation remains robust.

The introduction of CO promotes the continuous conversion of [Cu–O ] back to [Cu–O ], thereby facilitating *H conversion toward H O from kinetic perspectives. To clarify the origin of this deactivation, please provide the Raman spectrum of the spent catalyst. Is there coke after the long-term reaction under 20 vol% C H /Ar? Many studies attribute EDH deactivation to coke formation or the consumption of lattice oxygen.
Response: We sincerely thank you for this important suggestion, which has helped us improve the manuscript. Following your comment, we have performed Raman spectroscopy on the spent catalyst after long-term testing under continuous-flow 20 vol% C H /Ar. The spectrum is now included in Fig. 3h (Please see the revised manuscript, page 6, Fig. 3) alongside those of catalysts used under PEDH and TEDH conditions (20 vol% C H /20 vol% CO /Ar). As shown in Fig. 3h, the spent catalyst from the 20 vol% C H /Ar test exhibits no detectable D band (~1350 cm-1) or G band (~1580 cm-1) signals, indicating the absence of significant coke formation. This result aligns with our earlier Raman data from batch-reactor tests in pure C H atmosphere (Supplementary Fig. 8), ruling out coke deposition as the primary cause of deactivation. Moreover, in situ NAP-XPS analysis (Fig. 5a) shows no appreciable increase in oxygen-vacancy concentration under C H atmosphere. Collectively, these findings suggest that the activity loss in this case stems mainly from *H surface coverage and the reduction of Cu2+ species, rather than from coke formation or lattice-oxygen consumption. The related discussion of these newly added Raman results has been included in the revised manuscript (Please see the revised manuscript, page 7).

Stability evaluation of Cu /TiO for TEDH at 550°C revealed low initial activity (ca. 1.2 mmol g-1 h-1) with rapid deactivation to 20% of the initial activity within 10 h (Fig. 3g).
